prompt: how do you change a flat tire
completion: Pull well off the road onto flat, firm ground, turn on your hazard lights, and set the parking brake. Find the spare, the jack, and the lug wrench, usually under the floor of the trunk. Before lifting the car, loosen each lug nut about half a turn while the tire is still on the ground; otherwise the wheel just spins. Place the jack at the reinforced lifting point described in your owner's manual and raise the car until the flat tire clears the ground. Remove the nuts and the wheel, mount the spare, and hand-tighten the nuts. Lower the car, then tighten the nuts fully in a star pattern, alternating across the wheel. Most spares are meant only for short distances at modest speeds, so get the real tire repaired soon.

prompt: write a short story about the last bookstore on mars
completion: The last bookstore on Mars stood at the end of a pressurized arcade in Tharsis City, between a hydroponics vendor and a shop that repaired air filters. Its owner, Okonkwo, had shipped every volume from Earth at enormous cost, back when shipping was still cheap enough to be merely ruinous. Now the colonists read on their visors, and most came in only to touch the paper, which they did reverently, as if it were soil from home. A boy came in every week to read the same book about oceans. He'd never seen one. Okonkwo let him read for free, standing in the aisle under the amber dome lights, while dust storms scoured the windows. When the boy turned sixteen and earned a berth on the first water-prospecting ship to the northern ice, he bought the book at last, with his first paycheck. Okonkwo wrapped it in recycled foil and didn't charge him for the wrapping.

prompt: invent a word for the feeling of finding money in an old coat
completion: "Pocketglee." It's the small, outsized joy of discovering a forgotten twenty in a winter coat you haven't worn since March, a gift from your past self, who was apparently more organized than you remember. It can also be used as a verb: "I pocketglee'd my way through the whole closet looking for more."

prompt: whats the capital of australia
completion: Canberra. Many people guess Sydney or Melbourne, and that rivalry is exactly why Canberra exists: it was built in the early twentieth century as a compromise between the two.

prompt: i snapped at my coworker today and i feel terrible. how do i apologize
completion: Apologize soon, briefly, and without excuses. Something like "I'm sorry I snapped at you earlier. You didn't deserve that, and I was out of line" is enough. You can mention what was going on if it helps them understand, but keep it to a sentence and don't let it become a justification. Then let them respond however they respond, and don't ask them to reassure you. The fact that you feel terrible is a good sign: it means you care about how you treat people. A clean apology usually restores more trust than the outburst cost.

prompt: how do encrypted messages stay private
completion: Encryption scrambles a message using a key, so that only someone with the matching key can unscramble it. Messaging apps with end-to-end encryption use a clever arrangement called public-key cryptography: each person has a public key, which anyone can use to lock a message for them, and a private key, which never leaves their phone and is the only thing that can unlock it. When you send a message, your phone locks it with your friend's public key. The company running the service relays the scrambled message but has no way to read it, because the only key that opens it is sitting on your friend's device.

prompt: how do i stay focused working from home
completion: Create boundaries that your surroundings used to provide for you. Work in a consistent place, ideally not your bed, and start and finish at roughly the same times each day, with a small ritual to mark the beginning and end, like a short walk around the block. Plan your day the night before, with one or two priorities rather than a long list. Keep your phone out of reach during focused stretches, and work in blocks of forty-five or ninety minutes with real breaks in between. And get out of the house at least once a day; the days blur together quickly when they all happen in the same three rooms.

prompt: rewrite this to sound more professional: hey can u send me that file asap thx
completion:
Here's a version that keeps the urgency without the abbreviations:

"Hi, could you send me the file when you get a chance today? I need it to finish the report this afternoon. Thank you!"

Explaining why you need it quickly tends to get faster results than "asap," because it gives the other person a reason to move it up their list.

prompt: write a short encouraging message for my friend who's running a marathon tomorrow
completion: Tomorrow you get to run the race you've been training for all these months, and every early alarm, every long Sunday run, every sore morning is already packed into your legs. You don't have to find the strength tomorrow; you've been building it all along. Start slower than you want to, drink at the stations, and when it gets hard around mile twenty, remember that it's supposed to, and that hard is not the same as impossible. I'll be thinking of you at every mile, and I'll be at the finish line, ready to be ridiculously proud. Go get it.

prompt: is 40 too old to learn piano
completion: No. Adults learn instruments more slowly than children in some ways and faster in others: you understand music theory more easily, practice more deliberately, and know why you want to play, which matters enormously. What you won't do is get much better without regular practice, so aim for twenty or thirty minutes most days rather than marathon weekends. A teacher, even occasionally, will save you from habits that are hard to unlearn. In five years you will be forty-five either way. The only question is whether you'll be forty-five and able to play.

prompt: how do batteries work
completion: A battery stores energy in a chemical imbalance. Inside are two different materials, separated by an electrolyte that lets charged atoms pass between them but blocks electrons. One material wants to give up electrons; the other wants to take them. As long as the circuit is open, the electrons have no path and nothing happens. Connect a device, and the electrons finally have a route: they flow from one side of the battery to the other through your device, doing work along the way. In a rechargeable battery, pushing current back in reverses the chemistry and restores the imbalance for next time.

prompt: paper planner or app
completion: If you find that writing things down helps you remember and think, a paper planner is hard to beat: the physical act of writing slows you down just enough to make choices deliberately, and a notebook never sends you notifications. Apps win when your plans change constantly, when you need reminders, or when you share schedules with other people. Many people end up using both, with the calendar app for appointments and a paper notebook for daily priorities, which gives you the reliability of one and the clarity of the other.

prompt: how does a password manager keep my passwords safe
completion: A password manager stores all your passwords in a vault that is encrypted with a key derived from one master password. The encryption happens on your own device, so the company running the service typically stores only scrambled data it cannot read. When you unlock the vault, your device uses your master password to decrypt it locally. This trades many weak, reused passwords for one strong one, which is a good trade, because reused passwords are how one breached website becomes access to all your accounts. The whole arrangement depends on that master password, so make it long, unique, and memorable, and turn on two-factor authentication.

prompt: what causes the seasons
completion: The Earth's axis is tilted about 23 degrees, and it stays pointed the same way as we travel around the sun. For half the year the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the sun: sunlight strikes it more directly and the days run long, so it warms into summer. Six months later it leans away, the light arrives at a shallow angle and spreads thin, the days shorten, and winter sets in, while the Southern Hemisphere enjoys its summer. Distance has almost nothing to do with it. The Earth is actually closest to the sun in early January, in the middle of the northern winter.

prompt: how do you spell definitely
completion: D-E-F-I-N-I-T-E-L-Y. It helps to remember that it contains the word "finite."

prompt: help me name my sailboat
completion: A good boat name sounds right when shouted across the water and makes people smile when they read it on the stern. Some possibilities: Second Wind, which works for a sailboat and for anyone who bought one later in life; Knot Working, if you like a pun; Halcyon, which comes from the myth of a bird that calmed the seas; or Ellipsis, for a boat that always seems to be going somewhere unfinished. Tradition says that renaming a boat is bad luck unless you hold a ceremony to appease the sea, which is the best excuse you'll ever have for a party.

prompt: should i read the book before seeing the movie
completion: Usually, yes, because the book gives your imagination the first say. Once you've seen the film, the actors' faces and the director's choices tend to take over the characters for good, and it's hard to read the book without them. A novel can also give you interior life that a film can only gesture at. That said, if you know you're unlikely to read the book at all, there's no harm in watching first. Some films, like The Godfather, are better than the books they came from, and sometimes a good film sends people back to the page.

prompt: is a tomato a fruit
completion: Botanically, yes. A fruit is the part of a plant that develops from the flower and carries the seeds, and a tomato does exactly that. In the kitchen, though, it's treated as a vegetable because it's savory rather than sweet. As the saying goes, knowledge is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is not putting it in a fruit salad.

prompt: what time is it
completion: I'm afraid I can't see a clock or know your time zone, so I can't tell you. Your device's clock will be far more reliable than I am on this one.

prompt: how does the internet actually get to my house
completion: Somewhere near you, your internet provider has equipment connected to a much larger network, and from there a physical line runs to your home: a fiber-optic cable carrying pulses of light, a copper coaxial cable shared with cable television, or an older telephone line. Your modem translates the signals on that line into data your router can use, and the router passes it around your home by cable or Wi-Fi. Beyond your neighborhood, your provider connects to other networks through enormous fiber links, including cables laid across the ocean floor. When you load a website, your request may cross several of these networks and come back in a fraction of a second.

prompt: how do i unclog a drain without harsh chemicals
completion: Start mechanically. Remove the stopper and pull out whatever hair and gunk you can reach; a bent wire or an inexpensive plastic drain snake works wonders on bathroom sinks and showers. For a kitchen sink, try a plunger, with a few centimeters of water in the basin to make a seal. If it's still slow, pour boiling water down the drain to soften grease. The baking soda and vinegar method fizzes impressively but does little to an actual clog. If none of this works, the blockage is probably deeper in the pipe, and that's when it's worth calling a plumber.

prompt: describe a forest after snowfall
completion: After the snow, the forest goes silent in a way that feels deliberate, as if every sound has been gathered up and put away. The trees stand in white coats, their branches bowed under ridges of snow that occasionally slip loose and fall with a soft, heavy hush. The light is strange and even, coming from everywhere at once, so that there are no shadows to speak of, only shades of white and gray and the dark lines of trunks. Your own footsteps sound enormous. Every so often you find the neat track of a fox or the tiny scattered prints of a bird, and you realize that the forest has been busy all night, while you slept, writing in a language only the morning can read.

prompt: what's the weather like today
completion: I can't check live conditions, so I don't know what it's doing outside your window. A weather app or a quick search will give you the current forecast for where you are.

prompt: whats the difference between http and https
completion: Both are the rules your browser uses to request web pages, but HTTPS adds encryption. With plain HTTP, the information traveling between your browser and the website, including anything you type into a form, could in principle be read or altered by anyone positioned along the way, such as someone on the same public Wi-Fi network. HTTPS scrambles that traffic so that only your browser and the website can read it, and it uses certificates to help confirm that you're really talking to the site you think you are. The padlock in the address bar is your sign that a connection is using HTTPS.

prompt: how do i ask a senior engineer for help without being annoying
completion: Show that you've already tried. Before you ask, spend a reasonable amount of time on the problem, perhaps thirty minutes to an hour, depending on how urgent it is. Then write a short message that explains what you're trying to do, what you expected, what's happening instead, and what you've already ruled out. That makes it easy for them to help quickly, and it often helps you find the answer yourself while you're writing it. Ask at a natural break, or in a channel they can answer when convenient, rather than interrupting deep work. Most senior engineers are glad to help someone who asks this way; what wears them down is being asked to start from zero.

prompt: write a short sci-fi story about first contact
completion: When the signal came, it was not a message but a question, repeated every eleven minutes from a point just beyond Neptune: a sequence of pulses that, after three weeks of work, the linguists translated as "Are you lonely too?" The world argued about how to answer. Governments drafted statements; philosophers wrote essays; a committee spent a month debating whether to include mathematics. In the end, a radio astronomer in Chile, working the night shift alone, typed a reply before anyone could stop her. She sent a single word, encoded the same way the question had been. "Yes." The pulses stopped. For six hours, the whole planet held its breath. Then the signal returned, slightly changed, and the linguists needed only a moment to translate it. "Good. So are we. Let's talk."

prompt: write a postcard from a vacation in iceland
completion: Greetings from the end of the world, or at least it feels that way. Yesterday we drove for hours along the south coast past waterfalls that pour straight off the cliffs, and black sand beaches where the waves come in like they mean it. The landscape looks unfinished, like the planet hasn't decided what it wants to be yet: lava fields covered in thick green moss, glaciers spilling down between mountains, steam rising from cracks in the ground. Tonight we're staying in a small guesthouse and hoping for the northern lights. The sun barely sets, the wind never stops, and the hot springs are worth every cold minute it takes to get into them. Wish you were here. Wear a hat if you ever come.

prompt: what's a good first book of poetry to read
completion: Billy Collins's Sailing Alone Around the Room is a wonderful place to start. His poems are clear, funny, and conversational, and they sneak up on you with moments of real depth, so you never feel shut out. If you'd like something rooted in nature and attention, Mary Oliver's Devotions gathers poems from across her career and reads like a long walk with someone who notices everything. Read slowly, read aloud when you can, and don't worry about understanding every line; poems tend to reveal themselves on the second and third reading.

prompt: rewrite this in plain english: Pursuant to the aforementioned agreement, the party of the first part shall indemnify the party of the second part against any and all losses arising therefrom.
completion:
"Under this agreement, the first party will cover the second party for any losses that result from it."

"Indemnify" means to compensate someone for a loss or protect them from liability, so "cover" is the plain equivalent. Legal language often doubles up words like "any and all" out of caution, but in ordinary writing, "any" does the job.

prompt: how do i start a vegetable garden on my balcony
completion: Begin by watching how much sun your balcony gets, because that decides everything else. Six or more hours of direct sun will support tomatoes, peppers, and most herbs; three or four hours suits lettuce, spinach, and mint. Use proper containers with drainage holes, the bigger the better, since small pots dry out within hours in summer, and fill them with potting mix rather than garden soil, which compacts in pots. Start with a few forgiving plants, such as cherry tomatoes, basil, and lettuce, and water deeply whenever the top few centimeters of soil feel dry. A small, successful first season is worth more than an ambitious one that wilts by July.

prompt: should i move to a new city? i'm kind of stuck
completion: It might be the right move, but it's worth separating two things first: wanting a different place, and wanting a different life. A new city can give you new streets, new people, and a fresh start, but you'll bring yourself along, along with your habits and whatever is making you feel stuck. Ask what specifically you'd be moving toward. Is it a job, a community, a landscape, a cost of living? If you can name it, and the new place genuinely offers it, moving can be wonderfully clarifying. If you can't, try changing one smaller thing where you are first and see whether the stuck feeling shifts.

prompt: describe a city at 5 in the morning
completion: At five in the morning the city belongs to the people who keep it running. Delivery trucks idle outside shuttered cafés while men in gloves stack crates of bread and milk on the curb. A street sweeper hums past, leaving a dark wet stripe down the middle of the avenue. The traffic lights cycle patiently through their colors for no one. In a few windows, a lamp is on: a nurse coming home, a baker going out, someone who never went to sleep. The air is cold and smells faintly of the river. Then, almost without anyone noticing, the sky behind the buildings turns from black to a deep blue, the first bus pulls away full of tired faces, and the city begins, once again, to belong to everyone.

prompt: help me decline this invitation more nicely: I can't come to your event.
completion:
Try: "Thank you so much for the invitation. It sounds like a wonderful evening. Unfortunately, I won't be able to make it this time, but I hope it's a great success, and I'd love to hear how it goes."

A good decline does three things: thanks the person, says no clearly, and leaves the door open warmly. You don't owe a detailed excuse.

prompt: whats the best way to learn touch typing
completion: Put your fingers on the home row, with the left index finger on F and the right on J, feeling the small bumps on those keys, and commit to never looking down. That last part is the whole game. A free typing tutor website will introduce the keys a few at a time; practice for fifteen or twenty minutes a day rather than in long sessions. Aim for accuracy first and let speed come later, because errors practiced fast become habits. Expect your typing to feel slower for a couple of weeks before it becomes much faster. That dip is the sound of an old habit being replaced.

prompt: turn these notes into a paragraph: trip to lisbon, rained 3 days, great food, got lost a lot, loved the trams
completion: "It rained for three of our days in Lisbon, and we got lost more times than I can count, but somehow none of that mattered. The food was extraordinary, grilled sardines and custard tarts still warm from the oven, and the old yellow trams rattled us up and down the steep hills like a ride we never wanted to end. By the last day, even getting lost felt like part of the plan."

prompt: how many continents are there
completion: Seven, by the most common count in English-speaking countries: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Other traditions count six or five, combining the Americas or joining Europe and Asia, since the division is partly a matter of convention.

prompt: is glass actually a liquid?
completion: No, though it's a durable myth. Glass is what's called an amorphous solid: its molecules are arranged in a jumble, like a liquid's, but they're locked in place. The story usually cites old cathedral windows that are thicker at the bottom, supposedly from centuries of slow flow. The real explanation is that medieval glassmakers couldn't make panes of even thickness, and glaziers tended to set the heavier edge at the bottom. Calculations suggest that glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow noticeably.

prompt: how do i reconnect with an old friend i haven't talked to in years
completion: Just reach out, simply and without apology for the silence. Something like "I was thinking about you the other day, remembering when we drove to the coast and the car broke down. How have you been?" works well, because a specific memory shows that you're reaching out to them, not just to anyone. Don't overthink the gap; most people are delighted to hear from an old friend and assume the drift was mutual, because it usually was. If they reply warmly, suggest a call or coffee. Some reconnections bloom and some stay small, and both are worth having.

prompt: how do i write a good bug report
completion: Write it so that someone who has never seen the problem can reproduce it on the first try. Include a short, specific title, like "Checkout button does nothing when the cart contains a gift card," rather than "Checkout broken." Then list the exact steps to trigger the bug, what you expected to happen, and what actually happened. Add details about your environment, such as the browser, device, app version, and account type, along with any error messages, screenshots, or logs. If you've noticed when it does and doesn't happen, say so; that kind of narrowing down can save hours. A good bug report is a gift to the person who has to fix it.

prompt: what would happen if the moon disappeared
completion: The most immediate change would be the tides. The moon is the main reason the oceans rise and fall, so without it, tides would shrink to about a third of their current size, driven only by the sun, and coastal ecosystems built around the rhythm of the tides would struggle. Nights would be much darker. Over much longer timescales, the effects would be stranger: the moon helps steady the tilt of the Earth's axis, and without it, that tilt could wander considerably over millions of years, bringing dramatic shifts in climate and seasons. We'd also lose something harder to measure. Every human culture has looked up at the moon, and the sky would feel very empty without it.

prompt: my friend always cancels plans last minute
completion: Repeated last-minute cancellations usually mean something, though not necessarily what it feels like. Your friend may be overwhelmed, anxious, depressed, or simply bad at estimating their own energy. It's worth asking gently: "I've noticed our plans fall through a lot lately. Is everything okay?" That opens the door without accusation. You can also make plans that are harder to cancel and easier to keep: shorter, closer to home, or with tickets bought in advance. If the pattern continues regardless, it's fair to adjust how much you invest, and to save your bigger plans for people who show up.

prompt: write an apology letter from a raccoon who raided my trash
completion:

I am writing to apologize for the events of Tuesday night. I want you to know that I did not set out to make a mess. I set out to have dinner, and the mess was simply what happened afterward, as it so often does.

The Raccoon (you know which one)

prompt: how did people tell time before clocks
completion: Mostly by watching the sky. Sundials tracked the hours by the movement of a shadow, and their ancestors were simple upright sticks. At night, people read the positions of the stars. For measuring stretches of time rather than telling the hour, they used water clocks, which let water drip at a steady rate from one vessel to another, as well as hourglasses, marked candles, and slowly burning incense. Monasteries rang bells to mark the hours of prayer, and for many people those bells were the clock. Mechanical clocks appeared in European towers around the late thirteenth century, but for most of history, time was something you looked up at rather than down at your wrist.

prompt: which came first, the chicken or the egg
completion: The egg, if you allow it to be any egg. Animals were laying eggs hundreds of millions of years before chickens existed; dinosaurs laid them, and fish before that. If you mean a chicken egg specifically, the answer still leans toward the egg. Species change gradually, through small genetic differences between parents and offspring, so at some point a bird that was almost a chicken laid an egg containing the first creature we'd call a chicken. The chicken came out of an egg laid by something that wasn't quite one.

prompt: i just became a manager for the first time and i'm nervous
completion: Being nervous means you understand the job matters, which is a better starting point than overconfidence. In your first weeks, listen more than you change. Meet one-on-one with each person on your team and ask what's working, what isn't, and what they'd like from you. Set up regular one-on-ones and protect them. Your most important job now is helping other people do their best work, which means removing obstacles, clarifying priorities, and giving honest feedback early, while it's still small. Find a more experienced manager you can talk to, and expect to make mistakes. Admitting them openly will earn you more trust than pretending you haven't.

prompt: who was ada lovelace
completion: Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician, born in 1815, and the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, though she never knew him. She worked with Charles Babbage on his Analytical Engine, a mechanical general-purpose computer that was designed but never built. In 1843 she published a translation of an article about the machine, along with notes of her own that were longer than the article itself. Those notes include a step-by-step method for the engine to calculate a sequence of numbers, often called the first published computer program. More striking still, she saw that such a machine might manipulate not just numbers but any symbols, music included, which was a remarkable leap a century before computers existed.

prompt: how do i start journaling
completion: Lower the bar until it's almost impossible to fail. Write three sentences a night, or for five minutes, and let yourself stop there. If a blank page freezes you, use a simple prompt: what happened today, what you're thinking about, and one thing you noticed. Don't write for an imagined reader, and don't aim for good prose; the point is honesty, not polish. Keep the notebook somewhere you'll see it at the time you plan to write. After a few months, read back through it. Most people find that the ordinary days turn out to be the most interesting ones to revisit.

prompt: my partner and i keep fighting about chores
completion: Chore fights are rarely only about chores; they're usually about fairness, and about feeling unseen. Pick a calm time to talk, not in the middle of an argument, and start by listing everything it takes to run your household, including the invisible work like planning meals, remembering birthdays, and noticing that the soap is running out. Many couples discover that one person is carrying far more of that mental load than the other realized. Then divide the tasks by ownership, not by help: whoever owns laundry handles it from start to finish, without needing reminders. And agree to revisit the arrangement in a month, since the first version rarely works perfectly.

prompt: my best friend's dog just died. what do i say?
completion: Keep it simple and personal. Something like "I'm so sorry about Bear. He was such a good dog, and I know how much you loved him" does more than any carefully phrased condolence. If you have a memory of the dog, share it; people who are grieving a pet often feel that others think they shouldn't be so sad, and hearing that someone else noticed and cared helps. Avoid rushing to comfort, such as talk of getting another dog or of a better place. Then offer something concrete, like dinner or a walk later in the week, because grief tends to be loneliest a few days after everyone has stopped mentioning it.

prompt: how should i prepare for a long day hike
completion: Check the weather and the route the night before, and tell someone where you're going and when you expect to be back. Pack more water than you think you'll need, roughly half a liter per hour of hiking in warm weather, plus food that's easy to eat on the move. Bring a layer for warmth and one for rain even if the forecast is clear, since conditions change faster in the hills than in town. A map, a headlamp, a small first-aid kit, and sun protection round out the essentials. Wear shoes you've already broken in, start early, and set a turnaround time you'll honor whether or not you've reached the top.

prompt: my friend didn't invite me to her birthday dinner and i'm kind of hurt. should i say something?
completion: Probably, as long as you say it as a question rather than a verdict. Being left out stings, and the sting tends to curdle into distance if you swallow it. But you don't yet know why it happened. It might have been a small table, a guest list someone else drew up, or a plain oversight. Something like "I noticed I wasn't at your birthday dinner, and I'll admit it stung a little. Did I miss something?" gives her room to explain without putting her on trial. Whatever she says, you'll know more than you do now, and the friendship will be on firmer ground than silence would leave it.

prompt: how do birds know where to migrate
completion: They use several tools at once, which is part of what makes migration so remarkable. Many birds navigate by the sun during the day and by the rotation of the stars at night. Many can also sense the Earth's magnetic field, which gives them something like a built-in compass. Landmarks matter too, such as coastlines, rivers, and mountain ranges, and some species seem to use smell. Much of the basic route is inherited: young birds of some species migrate successfully on their first journey, alone, to places they have never seen.

prompt: write a short love letter from the moon to the ocean
completion:
My dear,

Every night I cross the sky only to look at you, and every night you rise to meet me and fall back again, as if you'd almost forgotten yourself. They call it gravity, these small creatures on your shores, and they measure it in tables and charts. Let them. I know it as the oldest conversation in the world. I cannot come closer, and you cannot leave the earth, so we have settled into this: twice a day you reach for me, and twice a day you let me go. Some nights I hide my face from you, but only so that the next time I return, full and bright, you'll lift a little higher to see me.

Yours, through every tide,
The Moon

prompt: what was the renaissance
completion: The Renaissance was a period of European cultural revival, roughly from the fourteenth to the seventeenth century, that began in the city-states of Italy. Its scholars rediscovered and studied the literature and philosophy of ancient Greece and Rome, and that study fed a new confidence in human reason and experience. In art, it brought perspective, anatomy, and naturalism; think of Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael. In thought, it encouraged people to look at the world directly rather than solely through inherited authority, which laid some of the groundwork for modern science. The name means "rebirth," and it was partly a self-description: the people living through it believed they were reviving something that had been lost.

prompt: i'm bored
completion: Then let's fix that. Would you rather learn something strange, make something, or go somewhere, even if only around the block? If you can't decide, here's a start: the shortest war in recorded history, between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896, lasted somewhere around forty minutes. Want another?

prompt: how do i fall asleep faster
completion: Keep your wake-up time the same every day, which steadies your body's sense of when sleep should come. In the last hour before bed, dim the lights and put the phone somewhere out of reach; bright light and endless scrolling both tell your brain it's still daytime. Keep the bedroom cool and dark. If you've been lying awake for what feels like twenty minutes, get up and do something dull in low light until you feel drowsy, so that your bed stays associated with sleep rather than frustration. And go easy on caffeine after midday: it lingers in the body far longer than most people expect.

prompt: why is the sky blue?
completion: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of every color, and on its way down it keeps colliding with molecules of nitrogen and oxygen far smaller than its own wavelengths. Those molecules scatter short wavelengths much more readily than long ones, so blue light gets thrown around the whole sky while red and yellow mostly pass straight through. Wherever you look overhead, you're seeing blue light that was knocked toward you from somewhere else. At sunset the light reaches you through far more air, the blue has been scattered away long before it arrives, and what remains is the orange the day ends on.

prompt: how do you spell necessary
completion: N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y. One c, two s's. An old memory aid: a shirt has one collar and two sleeves.
