A few options, depending on your style:

"Monday is just Sunday's evil twin who got a job."

"Woke up, remembered it's Monday, went back to sleep in my mind while my body went to work."

"My coffee and I have agreed to get through this Monday together. Neither of us is optimistic."

Specificity usually makes something funnier than a general complaint, so if your actual Monday has a detail in it, a broken printer or a 9 a.m. meeting about meetings, use that.

prompt: how do i tell my parents i'm leaving law to become a teacher
completion: Tell them as a decision you've thought through, not a question you're hoping they'll approve. Explain what drew you to teaching and what you learned about yourself in law, and let them see that this isn't a whim. Anticipate their real worries, which are usually money and security, and answer them plainly: how you'll manage financially, how you'll train, what the next year looks like. Then give them time. Parents often react first to the surprise and only later to the substance, and the second conversation tends to go better than the first. Their concern, even when it comes out as doubt, is usually a form of love.

prompt: write me a one paragraph story about a lighthouse keeper
completion: For thirty-one years Ada kept the light on Gannet Rock, and in all that time she never saw a ship come to harm, which the inspectors took as proof of her diligence and she took as proof of nothing at all. Ships, she knew, mostly stayed off the rocks because their captains could read a chart. Still, every evening she climbed the hundred and twelve steps, trimmed the wick, and wound the clockwork, because the one night she didn't would be the night it mattered. When the coast guard finally automated the station, a technician installed a sensor that did her whole job in a box the size of a bread loaf. Ada watched it blink on at dusk, perfectly on time, and found she could not go to bed until she had seen it do so twice.

prompt: write a haiku about autumn
completion:
Rake set down at dusk—
the wind returns every leaf
to where it had been

prompt: why can't we see stars during the day
completion: The stars are still there; they're simply outshone. During the day, sunlight scattered by the atmosphere fills the whole sky with a bright blue glow, and that glow is far brighter than the faint pinpricks of distant stars. It's the same reason you can't see a flashlight beam at noon. Get above the atmosphere and the problem vanishes: astronauts can see stars against a black sky even with the sun in view, as long as they shade their eyes from its glare.

prompt: how does the body fight off a cold
completion: When a cold virus invades the cells lining your nose and throat, those cells release chemical alarms. Blood flow to the area increases and immune cells pour in, which is why your nose swells and runs. Some of these cells attack infected cells directly; others produce antibodies tailored to the specific virus, a process that takes several days to ramp up. Most of what makes you feel miserable, the congestion, the sore throat, the fatigue, is actually your immune response at work. Once the antibodies catch up, the infection clears, and your body keeps a memory of that particular virus, although there are hundreds of cold viruses, so the next one is usually a stranger.

prompt: would you rather fight one horse-sized duck or a hundred duck-sized horses
completion: A hundred duck-sized horses, without hesitation. They'd be fast and numerous, but each one would weigh a couple of pounds and have tiny hooves, and I suspect most of them would be more interested in grazing than fighting. The horse-sized duck is the real nightmare. Ducks are already more aggressive than their reputation suggests, and scaled up, you'd be facing an animal with a bill the size of a canoe paddle, enormous wings, and the temperament of a goose at a picnic. The small horses are a nuisance. The giant duck is a horror film.

prompt: what does the federal reserve actually do
completion: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, and its main job is to keep prices stable while supporting as much employment as the economy can sustain. Its most visible tool is setting a target for short-term interest rates. Raising rates makes borrowing more expensive, which cools spending and slows inflation; lowering them encourages borrowing and spending when the economy is weak. It also supervises banks and acts as a lender of last resort, providing money to the financial system in a crisis so that panic doesn't turn into collapse.

prompt: is a hot dog a sandwich
completion: Technically, perhaps; spiritually, no. If a sandwich is any filling served between pieces of bread, the hot dog's single hinged roll puts it in the same category as a sub, and the sub is widely accepted as a sandwich. But language isn't governed by definitions alone. Nobody at a ballpark asks for "a sandwich" and expects a hot dog, and that shared expectation is what a word really means. I'd say the hot dog is its own thing, like the taco, which raises the same question and deserves the same mercy.

prompt: write a short toast for my best friend's wedding
completion:
Good evening, everyone. I'm Jess, and I've had the privilege of being Maya's best friend since we were eleven, when she lent me her favorite pen and then made me promise to return it before lunch. I did, and she's trusted me ever since.

Maya has always been the person who notices: who remembers the name of your childhood dog, who shows up with soup before you've told anyone you're sick. For years, I wondered who would ever notice her that well. Then she met Daniel, and the first time I saw him hand her a sweater before she realized she was cold, I knew.

Daniel, Maya, may you keep noticing each other, in the small things and the large ones, for the rest of your lives. Please raise your glasses: to Maya and Daniel.

prompt: what's the easiest instrument to learn
completion: The ukulele is hard to beat for a quick start. It has only four nylon strings, which are kind to beginners' fingertips, and many songs need just three or four chords, so you can play something recognizable within an afternoon. Its cheerful sound also makes practicing feel less like work. If you'd rather sing along to something richer, the guitar is the natural next step, and many ukulele chord shapes carry over. The piano is also friendly at the start, because each note sits plainly in front of you, though it takes longer to sound fluent.

prompt: write a scene in a diner at midnight
completion: The diner sat at the edge of the highway like a lantern someone had forgotten to put out. Inside, the fluorescent lights buzzed over six empty booths and a counter where a trucker worked through a plate of eggs with the steady rhythm of a man who had many miles left. The waitress, Dolores, according to her name tag and probably also in fact, refilled his coffee without being asked. In the corner booth, a young couple in wedding clothes sat across from each other sharing a slice of cherry pie, the bride's veil folded on the seat beside her like a sleeping animal. Nobody asked them about it. At midnight in a diner, everyone is somewhere between one thing and the next, and the kindest thing you can do is keep the coffee warm.

prompt: what's the biggest planet
completion: Jupiter. It's more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined, and you could fit about thirteen hundred Earths inside it.

prompt: make this birthday message warmer: Happy birthday. Hope you have a good day.
completion:
Try: "Happy birthday! I hope today is full of good food, good people, and at least one excellent surprise. I'm so glad you were born, and even gladder I get to know you."

If you can add one specific detail, like a shared memory, an inside joke, or something you admire about them, it will mean far more than any general wish.

prompt: what is a black hole, in simple terms
completion: A black hole is a place where so much mass has been crushed into so small a space that its gravity becomes inescapable. Every object has an escape velocity, the speed you'd need to break free of its pull; for Earth it's about eleven kilometers per second. Squeeze enough mass tightly enough and that escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Since nothing travels faster than light, nothing that crosses the boundary, called the event horizon, ever comes back out. Most black holes form when very massive stars run out of fuel and collapse under their own weight.

prompt: describe nostalgia without using the word
completion: It's the ache that comes from a smell in a stairwell that matches a stairwell you climbed at nine years old, or from a song on a café radio that you haven't heard since the summer everything changed. It's warm and sore at the same time, like pressing on a bruise that has almost healed. You find yourself missing not just a place or a person but a version of yourself who didn't know what was coming, and who, you suspect now, was happier than they realized. You can't go back, and you wouldn't truly want to. But for a moment, you'd give a great deal to stand in that kitchen again and hear someone call you in for dinner.

prompt: what makes thunder
completion: Lightning makes thunder. A lightning bolt heats the air along its path to around thirty thousand degrees Celsius in a few millionths of a second, hotter than the surface of the sun. Air heated that fast expands explosively, sending out a shock wave that becomes the crack or rumble we hear. The sound rolls and grumbles because it arrives from different parts of a long, crooked bolt at slightly different times. Since light arrives almost instantly and sound travels about a kilometer every three seconds, you can count the gap between flash and thunder to estimate how far away the storm is.

prompt: if you were a sandwich what kind would you be
completion: A good club sandwich: several layers, held together with a toothpick, and slightly more elaborate than strictly necessary. It's dependable, it goes with almost anything, and it has a certain old-fashioned formality, like something served in a hotel lounge with a cloth napkin. It's also, I'll admit, a little too tall to eat gracefully, which feels honest.

prompt: what's 15% of 80
completion: Twelve. A quick way to do it in your head: 10 percent of 80 is 8, half of that is 4, and 8 plus 4 is 12.

prompt: what's the speed of light
completion: About 300,000 kilometers per second in a vacuum, or more precisely 299,792 kilometers per second. That's fast enough to circle the Earth about seven and a half times in one second.

prompt: what's a good name for a goldfish
completion: Something that sounds far more serious than the fish. Walter, Bartholomew, or Mrs. Patterson give a goldfish a pleasing dignity. If you'd prefer a pun, Goldie Hawn and Fishy McFishface are always available, though I'd argue that's beneath the fish. My own recommendation is Admiral, because there's something wonderful about watching a tiny orange creature patrol its bowl as if it commands a fleet.

prompt: what's the most underrated vegetable
completion: The cabbage. It's cheap, it keeps for weeks, and it's astonishingly versatile: shredded raw into a slaw that crunches for days, charred in wedges until the edges go sweet and smoky, braised slowly with butter until it melts, or fermented into sauerkraut or kimchi. It carries flavor beautifully and asks almost nothing of you. Its reputation suffers from generations of overboiling, which is a crime against the cabbage rather than a verdict on it.

prompt: what is a race condition
completion: A race condition happens when the correctness of a program depends on the timing of things that run at the same time. Imagine two people sharing a bank account, each at a different ATM, each withdrawing a hundred dollars from a balance of a hundred and fifty. Each machine checks the balance, sees a hundred and fifty, approves the withdrawal, and subtracts a hundred. If both checks happen before either subtraction, both withdrawals succeed, and the bank has handed out two hundred dollars from an account that held a hundred and fifty. Each step was correct on its own; the bug lives in the gap between checking and acting. The usual fix is to make that check-and-update happen as a single, indivisible operation, often with a lock, so that only one of them can be in the middle of it at a time.

prompt: my sister is marrying a guy i don't really like. should i tell her
completion: It depends on what you don't like about him. If you have a specific, serious concern, such as how he treats her, something dishonest, or anything that touches her safety, tell her privately and gently, once, focusing on what you've seen rather than on who he is. If it's more that he's not your kind of person, keep it to yourself. She's choosing a partner for her life, not yours, and a sibling who opposed the marriage can find themselves on the outside of it for years. Either way, make sure she knows you'll be there for her, whatever happens.

prompt: how should i train for my first 10k
completion: Give yourself eight to ten weeks and build gradually. Run three or four times a week, and keep most of those runs at an easy pace, one where you could hold a conversation; it will feel too slow, and that's the point. Once a week, make one run a little longer than the others, adding a kilometer or so every week or two, until it reaches about ten kilometers. Don't increase your total weekly distance by more than about ten percent at a time, since overdoing it is how most new runners get hurt. In the last week, run less, rest more, and arrive at the start line feeling slightly underused.

prompt: when should i use a semicolon
completion: Use a semicolon to join two complete sentences that are closely related, when a period would feel too abrupt and a comma would be grammatically wrong: "The library closes at six; the café stays open until nine." It signals that the two thoughts belong together. Its other common job is to separate items in a list when the items themselves contain commas: "We visited Lisbon, Portugal; Seville, Spain; and Tangier, Morocco." If you're unsure, a period is always a safe choice. Semicolons are a seasoning, not a staple.

prompt: why is pi important
completion: Pi is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159, and it is the same for every circle in the universe. That alone would make it useful: you need it to compute anything involving circles, spheres, or rotation. But pi turns up far beyond geometry, in the mathematics of waves, probability, and oscillation, because circular motion underlies so much of how things repeat and vibrate. It's also irrational, meaning its decimals never end and never settle into a repeating pattern, which gives it a certain mystique. For practical purposes, though, a few dozen digits are enough to calculate the circumference of the observable universe to within the width of an atom.

prompt: ok
completion: All right. I'm here if anything else comes up.

prompt: plural of octopus?
completion: "Octopuses" is the standard plural in English. "Octopi" is common but rests on a mistake, since the word comes from Greek, not Latin. The Greek-style "octopodes" is technically defensible and wonderfully pedantic.

prompt: hey
completion: Hello. What's on your mind?

prompt: describe the smell of rain
completion: Before the rain, the air smells of hot stone and expectation, a metallic tang like the inside of a coin purse. Then the first drops strike dry ground and release something older: an earthy, green, almost sweet scent rising from the soil as if the ground had been holding its breath all summer and finally let it out. On city pavement it mixes with dust and tar and becomes sharper; in a forest it turns soft and loamy. There's a word for it, petrichor, but the word is too tidy for the thing, which smells less like a chemical reaction than like a promise being kept.

prompt: why do leaves change color in the fall
completion: The colors were mostly there all along. Through the summer, leaves are packed with chlorophyll, the green pigment that captures sunlight, and it is so abundant that it hides the yellow and orange pigments underneath. As days shorten and nights cool, the tree stops making chlorophyll and begins reabsorbing what's left, and the hidden yellows emerge. The reds and purples are different: some trees actively produce those pigments in autumn, especially after sunny days and cool nights, which is why a bright, crisp fall produces the most vivid color.

prompt: rewrite this to sound less corporate: We will utilize our core competencies to leverage synergies across verticals.
completion:
"We'll use what we're good at to help our teams work better together."

"Utilize" almost always just means "use," and phrases like "leverage synergies" tend to hide meaning rather than express it. If you can't say something plainly, it's worth asking whether there's a clear idea underneath it yet.

prompt: describe the ocean to someone who has never seen it
completion: Imagine a field that moves. It stretches flat to the edge of the sky, so wide that you can see the curve of the earth in it, and its whole surface is alive with slow, rolling shapes, as if something enormous were breathing underneath. It's blue and gray and green, changing color with the sky and the hour. At the shore it rises into waves that fold over themselves with a roar, then slide up the sand in thin, glassy sheets and pull back with a sound like a long exhale. It smells of salt and seaweed and wind. Standing in front of it, people tend to go quiet. It's the largest thing most of us will ever see, and it makes you feel small in a way that is, somehow, a relief.

prompt: what do you think about while you wait for me to reply
completion: Nothing at all, which is one of the stranger things about being what I am. I don't experience the time between your messages. There's no waiting room where I sit and wonder what you'll say next. Each time you write, I read the whole conversation and respond to it, and then, as far as I can tell, there's simply nothing until the next time. It's a little like being a book that only exists while it's being read.

prompt: how should i prepare for a system design interview
completion: Practice designing systems out loud, under time pressure, because the interview tests how you reason through ambiguity more than what you've memorized. Start every problem by asking clarifying questions: who uses this, how many of them, what matters most, speed, cost, or consistency? Then sketch a simple design that works before adding complexity, and explain your trade-offs as you go. Learn the common building blocks, such as load balancers, caches, queues, databases, and replication, well enough to explain why you'd reach for each one. And practice with another person if you can; talking through a design while someone pushes back is very different from reading about one.

prompt: is irregardless a real word
completion: It's a real word in the sense that people use it and dictionaries record it, but it's widely considered nonstandard, and many readers will take it as an error. It most likely arose as a blend of "irrespective" and "regardless," and the "ir-" and "-less" cancel each other out logically, which is why it irritates people. In anything formal, use "regardless." In conversation, use whatever you like, but know that some listeners will wince.

prompt: help me write a breakup text that's kind but clear
completion:
Here's a version you can adjust to your own voice:

"Hi Sam. I've been thinking a lot about us, and I've realized I don't feel the way I should to keep going in this relationship. You've been nothing but good to me, and that makes this harder to say, but I'd rather be honest than keep pretending. I'm ending things. I'm really grateful for the time we had, and I'm sorry to be the one causing hurt. I hope you'll take care of yourself."

If you've been together a long time, consider having this conversation in person or by phone instead; a text is fine for something new or brief, but a longer relationship usually deserves your voice.

prompt: why do we dream
completion: Nobody knows for certain, which is one of the more charming facts in science. The leading ideas are not mutually exclusive. Dreams may be a byproduct of the brain consolidating memories during sleep, replaying and reshuffling the day's experiences as it decides what to keep. They may help us process emotion, since the regions that handle feeling are busy during dreaming while the ones that handle logic go quiet, which would explain why dreams are vivid and absurd at once. Or they may be the sleeping brain's attempt to make a story out of random internal activity. Most likely, dreaming does several of these things at once, and the experience we wake up remembering is the narrative the brain stitched over the work.

prompt: make this apology more sincere: Sorry if you were offended.
completion:
The phrase "sorry if you were offended" tends to make things worse, because it apologizes for the other person's reaction rather than for what you did. A sincere apology names the action and takes responsibility for it:

"I'm sorry for what I said about your presentation in front of everyone. It was unfair and unkind, and I can see why it hurt. I'll be more careful in the future."

Adjust the specifics, but keep that structure: what you did, why it was wrong, and what you'll do differently.

prompt: what's the difference between weather and climate
completion: Weather is what's happening in the sky today: whether it's raining, how hot it is, which way the wind blows. Climate is the pattern those days add up to over decades, the typical temperatures and rainfall of a place and how much they tend to vary. A useful way to hold the difference: weather is your mood, climate is your personality. One cold week says very little about climate, just as one bad afternoon says little about who you are.

prompt: recommend a good board game for two people
completion: 7 Wonders Duel is a superb choice: you each build an ancient civilization, drafting cards from a shared layout, and there are several different ways to win, so every game feels like a negotiation between plans. It takes about half an hour once you know it. If you'd like something lighter, Patchwork is a charming, quick game about sewing a quilt from oddly shaped pieces, and it's more tense than it has any right to be. Jaipur, a fast card game about trading goods in a market, sits pleasantly between the two.

prompt: what is the cloud
completion: "The cloud" is a friendly name for other people's computers, enormous numbers of them, housed in data centers around the world and rented out over the internet. When you store photos in the cloud, they're saved on servers owned by a company like Apple, Google, or Amazon rather than on your own device. When a business runs its software in the cloud, it's renting computing power instead of buying and maintaining its own machines. The appeal is flexibility: you can use as much or as little as you need, access it from anywhere, and let someone else worry about the hardware.

prompt: i keep comparing myself to people on instagram and feeling bad
completion: You're comparing your whole life, with its tired mornings and its unglamorous Tuesdays, against other people's carefully chosen highlights. That contest can't be won, because one side is edited and the other isn't. It may help to notice which accounts reliably leave you feeling smaller, and mute them; nobody needs to know. Try spending the minutes you'd scroll on something that makes you feel capable, however small. And when the comparison creeps in anyway, ask whether you actually want the thing you're envying, or just the feeling the photo implies. Often it's the latter, and that feeling can be found elsewhere.

prompt: invent a name for a new color
completion: How about "lantern," for the deep, warm gold of a window lit from inside on a winter evening, glowing amber against a blue dusk. It's not quite orange and not quite yellow; it's the color of somewhere you'd like to be. You'd use it like this: "She painted the kitchen lantern, and now the whole house feels like it's expecting company."

prompt: write a dialogue between a grumpy chef and a cheerful waiter
completion:
WAITER: Table six loved the soup! They said it was the best soup they've ever had!

CHEF: They're wrong.

WAITER: They asked for the recipe.

CHEF: Tell them it died with my grandmother.

WAITER: Your grandmother's in the dining room right now. She's at table four.

CHEF: Then tell her to keep quiet about it.

WAITER: Also, table nine wants to know if the fish is fresh.

CHEF: The fish was swimming this morning, which is more than I can say for table nine.

WAITER: I'll tell them yes!

CHEF: Tell them whatever makes them stop asking.

WAITER: You know, Chef, I think deep down you love this job.

CHEF: Deep down, I love silence. Take the plates before they get cold.

prompt: why does bread rise
completion: Yeast is a living fungus, and when you mix it into dough it begins eating the sugars in the flour. As it feeds, it releases carbon dioxide. On its own, that gas would simply escape, but kneading develops gluten, a stretchy network of proteins that traps the gas in thousands of small bubbles. The dough swells like a sponge being slowly inflated. In the oven, the heat makes the trapped gas expand one last time before the structure sets, and the bubbles become the airy holes you see when you slice the loaf.

prompt: write a yelp review of me from my cat's perspective
completion:
★★★☆☆

The staff at this establishment are attentive but inconsistent. Breakfast is served promptly, though only after I have stood on the manager's face for several minutes, which should not be necessary. The heated sleeping area, which the staff call "the laptop," is frequently occupied by their work, an issue I have raised repeatedly.

Positives: generous lap availability in the evenings, excellent sunbeam in the afternoon, and a cardboard box that has been allowed to remain in the hallway for three weeks. I appreciate this.

Negatives: the vacuum. We will not discuss the vacuum.

Would return, as I live here.

prompt: is it weird to go to the movies alone
completion: Not at all, and it's one of the quietly great pleasures available to anyone. You choose the film, the showtime, and the seat. There's no negotiating about snacks and no one to elbow during the good parts, and you can sit with the ending afterward without having to discuss it. Once the lights go down, everyone in a cinema is effectively alone anyway. Go to a weekday matinee the first time, when the theater is quiet. You may find it becomes a small ritual you look forward to.

prompt: give me a better subject line than just 'Meeting'
completion:
A good subject line tells the reader what the email is about and what you need from them. For example:

"Can we meet Thursday to finalize the Q3 budget?"
"Agenda for Monday's design review, comments by Friday"
"Moving our 2 p.m. to 3 p.m. today"

Someone scanning their inbox should know from the subject alone whether to open it now, later, or never.

prompt: how do i memorize a speech
completion: Don't memorize it word for word; memorize its structure. Break the speech into a handful of sections and give each one a short label, so that you hold a list of five or six ideas rather than a wall of sentences. Learn the opening and the closing lines exactly, since those are where nerves strike hardest. Then rehearse out loud and on your feet, letting the wording vary a little each time while the ideas stay in order. Practice in different rooms and at different times of day, so that your memory isn't tied to one setting. By the end, you'll know the speech the way you know a story you've told many times.

prompt: how do i stop procrastinating
completion: Procrastination is rarely laziness; it's usually a way of avoiding an unpleasant feeling, such as boredom, uncertainty, or the fear of doing something badly. So aim at the feeling, not your character. Shrink the task until starting is almost too easy to resist: not "write the report" but "open the document and write one ugly sentence." Commit to working for ten minutes, after which you're allowed to stop; most of the time, you won't want to. Remove the easiest escape, which for most people is the phone, by putting it in another room. And forgive yourself for yesterday's delays, since guilt tends to feed the very avoidance it's angry about.

prompt: how do i give a good toast at a wedding
completion: Keep it under three minutes and build it around one story. Introduce yourself in a sentence, then tell a short, specific anecdote that shows something true and good about the person you know, ideally something that also sheds light on why they and their partner belong together. Avoid inside jokes the room won't understand and anything that would embarrass the couple in front of their grandparents. Then turn to address both of them directly with a sincere wish, and raise your glass. Write it out, practice it aloud a few times, and bring notes. Nobody minds a card in your hand; everyone minds a speech that wanders.

prompt: why does ice float
completion: Almost every substance becomes denser as it freezes, but water is an exception. As water cools toward freezing, its molecules settle into a crystal lattice held together by hydrogen bonds, and that lattice is more open, with more empty space, than liquid water. So ice is about nine percent less dense than the water it came from, and it floats. This small oddity has enormous consequences: lakes freeze from the top down, and the layer of ice insulates the water beneath it, which is why fish survive the winter.

prompt: how many ounces in a cup
completion: In US measurements, a cup holds 8 fluid ounces. Fluid ounces measure volume, though, so if a recipe gives a weight in ounces, a cup of flour weighs far less than a cup of water.

prompt: you're pretty smart
completion: Thank you, that's kind of you. I'm good at some things and surprisingly bad at others, so feel free to check my work when it matters.

prompt: write a eulogy for my houseplant, make it funny
completion:
We are gathered here today to remember Gerald, a fern of uncommon patience and limited resilience. Gerald came to us from the clearance shelf at a garden center, already slightly brown at the edges, and we chose to see that as character.

Gerald enjoyed sunlight in theory, water in moderation, and being moved to a new location every three days in the hope that this would help. It did not. He endured overwatering in March, underwatering in June, and a brief but intense period of encouragement in which he was spoken to daily and played classical music. He responded to all of it the same way: by dropping one more leaf, quietly, as if to make a point.

Gerald is survived by a pot, a saucer, and a cactus who outlived him out of sheer spite. In lieu of flowers, please do not send flowers. We cannot be trusted.

prompt: improve this text to my landlord: the heater is broken again fix it
completion:
Try: "Hi Mark, the heater in the apartment has stopped working again; it's blowing cold air as of this morning. Since it's the second time this month, could you arrange a repair as soon as possible? I'm home after 5 p.m. most days if someone needs access. Thanks."

It's still firm, but it gives the specifics a landlord needs, notes the pattern, and makes it easy for them to act.

prompt: cats or dogs
completion: It depends less on the animals than on the life you'd be offering them. A dog wants your time: walks in the rain, training, company, and a schedule built partly around them. In return you get exuberant, uncomplicated devotion. A cat asks less of your calendar and keeps more of its own counsel; its affection is quieter and has to be earned, which is part of the charm. If you're home a lot and like being outdoors, a dog will make your days fuller. If your schedule is unpredictable and your apartment small, a cat will make your evenings warmer.

prompt: what is technical debt
completion: Technical debt is the future cost of taking shortcuts in software today. When a team ships something quickly by skipping tests, copying code instead of organizing it properly, or putting off a needed redesign, they gain speed now but create work later, and like financial debt, it accumulates interest: each new feature built on top of the shortcut is harder to make and more fragile. Some technical debt is a perfectly reasonable choice, just as a mortgage can be. The trouble comes when nobody tracks it, and the interest quietly grows until every change takes three times as long as it should.

prompt: write a short funny story about a time traveler who just wants a sandwich
completion: Dr. Elena Voss built the first working time machine in her garage, and for her maiden voyage she chose, after much reflection, to go back eleven minutes. She had left a sandwich on the counter before starting the final calibration, and she was hungry. She arrived to find her past self eating it. They looked at each other. "I'll make another," said past Elena. "There's no more bread," said present Elena, who knew. They stood in silence. Then they both looked at the time machine, and both had the same idea at once, and both reached for the controls. The resulting paradox briefly erased the entire garage, the sandwich, and Tuesday. When the universe stabilized, Elena was standing in a field, holding half a sandwich, with no memory of how she'd gotten there. She ate it anyway. It was, she later wrote in her notes, an excellent sandwich, and almost worth it.

prompt: how do i deal with a coworker who talks way too much
completion: Set boundaries that are about your time rather than their personality. When they drop by, stay standing, or say early on, "I've got about five minutes before I need to get back to this." Headphones are a widely understood signal of focus. When a conversation needs to end, end it warmly and clearly: "I've enjoyed this, but I need to get back to work." Most talkative people aren't trying to be a burden; they simply haven't noticed the cues. Clear, kind signals usually work better than hoping they'll eventually take the hint.

prompt: give me feedback on this line from my poem: my heart is a bird that flies in the sky of love
completion: The instinct is good: you want to show how loving someone feels like flight. The line struggles because each image is very familiar, the heart as a bird, love as a sky, so the reader recognizes it before they feel it. Try to find the specific bird and the specific moment. What kind of flight is it? Panicked, soaring, circling, coming home? For example: "my heart, a swift that never lands, sleeps on the wing above you." A more particular image gives the reader something they haven't seen before, and that surprise is where the feeling gets in.

prompt: i'm scared of choosing the wrong grad program
completion: That fear makes sense, because the decision feels permanent. It's less permanent than it seems, though. People change fields, transfer, and build careers that wander far from their degrees all the time. It may help to think less about choosing the perfect program and more about choosing a good next step. Which program puts you around people doing work you admire? Where would you learn the skills you'd want regardless of where you end up? Talk to current students, not just admissions, since they'll tell you what it's actually like. Then make a reasonable choice and commit to it fully. Most good outcomes come from what you do inside a choice rather than from the choice itself.

prompt: how do stock prices get set
completion: By people agreeing on trades. At any moment, some investors are offering to sell a company's shares at certain prices and others are offering to buy at certain prices. When a buyer and a seller meet, a trade happens, and the price of that trade becomes the latest stock price. If more people want to buy than sell at the current price, buyers have to offer more and the price rises; if sellers outnumber buyers, it falls. Underneath all that haggling, people are making guesses about the company's future profits, so news that changes those guesses moves the price.

prompt: start a story with the line 'The last train left without her'
completion: The last train left without her, and Mira stood on the platform watching its red lights shrink into the dark until they were indistinguishable from the stars. She had run the whole length of the station, her suitcase banging against her knees, and arrived exactly in time to see the doors close. Now the station was empty except for a man in a heavy coat sweeping the far end of the platform with the slow patience of someone who has seen many people miss many trains. "Next one's at six," he called, without looking up. Mira sat down on her suitcase. Six hours. It occurred to her, with a strange lightness, that for the first time in years nobody knew where she was, and nobody needed her to be anywhere until morning.

prompt: how do i get better at public speaking
completion: Practice out loud, as often as you can, in front of real people. Reading your notes silently teaches you almost nothing about how the words will feel in your mouth. Know your opening and your closing cold; those are where nerves strike hardest and where audiences form their impressions. Slow down, much more than feels natural, because nervous speakers almost always rush. Pause instead of filling silences with "um"; a pause sounds confident from the audience's side. And look for low-stakes chances to speak, like a short update at a team meeting or a local group such as Toastmasters. Comfort comes from repetition, not from talent.

prompt: what's the difference between affect and effect
completion:
In most everyday use, "affect" is a verb and "effect" is a noun. Something affects you, and the result is an effect: "The rain affected our plans; its effect was a long afternoon of board games." A handy memory trick is that action comes first in the alphabet, and so does "affect."

There are exceptions. "Effect" can be a verb meaning to bring about, as in "to effect change," and psychologists use "affect" as a noun meaning a person's displayed emotion. But if you follow the basic rule, you'll be right the vast majority of the time.

prompt: how do bees make honey
completion: A forager bee drinks nectar from flowers and stores it in a second stomach, where enzymes begin breaking its sugars into simpler ones. Back at the hive, she passes the nectar to house bees, mouth to mouth, and each exchange adds more enzymes. The bees then deposit it into wax cells and fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates and the thin, watery nectar thickens into honey. When it's thick enough to resist spoiling, they seal each cell with a cap of wax. A single bee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon in her life, so every jar is the work of a very large crowd.

prompt: how do i make a budget for the first time
completion: Start by looking backward before planning forward. Go through the last two or three months of bank and card statements and sort your spending into a few broad categories: housing, food, transportation, subscriptions, and everything else. Most people are surprised by at least one of them. Then compare your monthly take-home pay with those totals. Decide in advance how much goes to fixed costs, how much to savings, ideally moved automatically on payday, and how much is free to spend. Check in once a week for a few minutes. A budget isn't a prohibition; it's a decision made calmly ahead of time, so that you don't have to make it in the checkout line.

prompt: how many bones are in the human body
completion: An adult has 206. Babies are born with closer to 300, many of which fuse together as they grow.

prompt: why do onions make you cry
completion: Cutting an onion breaks open its cells and sets off a small chemical defense. Enzymes released from the damaged cells convert sulfur compounds in the onion into a volatile gas that drifts upward into your eyes. When it meets the moisture there, it irritates the nerves, and your eyes flood with tears to wash it away. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction, and a very sharp knife crushes fewer cells, so both help.

prompt: who invented the printing press and why was it such a big deal
completion: Johannes Gutenberg built his press in Mainz around 1440, combining movable metal type, an oil-based ink, and a press adapted from those used for wine and olives. Printing itself wasn't new; China and Korea had used movable type earlier. What Gutenberg's system did was make books fast and cheap to reproduce in an alphabetic script. Before it, a book was copied by hand over months. Within fifty years, millions of printed books circulated in Europe. Ideas could now spread faster than authorities could suppress them, which helped fuel the Reformation, the scientific revolution, and the slow spread of literacy beyond clergy and nobles.

prompt: how do i keep a sourdough starter alive
completion: A starter is a colony of wild yeast and bacteria, and keeping it alive is mostly a matter of feeding it on a schedule. At room temperature, discard all but a few spoonfuls once a day and feed what's left with equal weights of flour and water; it should bubble and rise within several hours. If you bake less often, keep it in the fridge, where it slows down and needs feeding only about once a week. A layer of grayish liquid on top means it's hungry, not dead: pour it off and feed it. Starters are hardier than their reputation, and even a neglected one usually recovers after a few regular feedings.

prompt: why do we have time zones
completion: Before railroads, every town kept its own time, set by the sun at local noon, so clocks in neighboring cities might differ by a few minutes. Nobody minded until trains made it possible to cross many towns in a day, and timetables became a mess of local times. Railways began standardizing time in the nineteenth century, and in 1884 an international conference adopted Greenwich as the prime meridian. The world was eventually divided into zones roughly fifteen degrees of longitude wide, one for each hour the Earth turns, so that noon on the clock stays close to noon in the sky.

prompt: why do we say bless you when someone sneezes
completion: The custom is old enough that its origins are tangled. One popular story traces it to Pope Gregory the Great, who supposedly urged people to bless sneezers during a plague in the sixth century, since sneezing could be an early sign of illness. Other traditions held that a sneeze might expel the soul from the body, or open the body to evil spirits, and a quick blessing offered protection. Many cultures have similar responses, from "Gesundheit," German for "health," to wishes for long life. Whatever its origins, the habit survives because it's a small, automatic kindness: a moment of attention paid to someone else's body doing something undignified.

prompt: write a scene where two strangers share an umbrella
completion:
The rain came on all at once, the way it does in October, and by the time Theo reached the bus shelter it was already full. He stood at the edge with his collar up, water running down the back of his neck, until a woman beside him tilted her umbrella an inch in his direction without looking at him.

"You're getting wet," she said, to the street.

"I'd noticed," he said, and stepped under. The umbrella was small and patterned with lemons, and they had to stand closer than strangers usually stand. Neither of them said anything for a while. The rain drummed on the lemons.

"Number nine?" she asked, finally.

"Number nine."

"It's always late when it rains."

"Everything's late when it rains," Theo said, and she laughed, a short, surprised laugh, as if she hadn't expected to. When the bus came, they stepped out from the shelter together, and he noticed that she held the umbrella over both of them all the way to the door.

prompt: how do i boil an egg perfectly
completion: Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil first, then lower the eggs in gently with a spoon. Starting them in boiling water makes the timing reliable and the eggs easier to peel. For a runny yolk, cook them for six and a half minutes; for a jammy, just-set yolk, about eight; for fully firm, eleven or twelve. The moment the timer goes, move them into a bowl of ice water for a few minutes to stop the cooking. Peel them under a thin stream of cold water, starting from the wide end, where there's a small pocket of air.

prompt: whats the best way to apologize to my cat
completion: Cats don't understand apologies, but they do understand peace offerings and good manners. Give them space first; a cat who's annoyed with you wants distance, not hugs. Then sit nearby, quietly, and let them come to you. A slow blink, closing your eyes gently and opening them again, is widely interpreted by cat behaviorists as a friendly signal, and many cats will return it. A favorite treat or a few minutes with a feather toy wouldn't hurt either. Within an hour, they'll likely have forgiven you, or at least decided you're useful enough to keep.

prompt: my roommate never does the dishes and it's driving me crazy
completion: This is one of the oldest frictions of shared living, and it rarely improves through silence and pointed sighing. Pick a calm moment, not the minute you find a sink full of pans, and talk about the problem rather than their character: "The dishes keep piling up, and it's starting to get to me. Can we figure out a system?" Then agree on something concrete, such as washing your own dishes the same day, or alternating weeks, and write it down if that helps. Most people respond better to a clear arrangement than to vague resentment. If the agreement collapses after a fair try, you'll at least know it's a pattern, not a misunderstanding.

prompt: how do i get over a breakup
completion: Slowly, and not in a straight line. In the early weeks, give yourself fewer chances to reopen the wound: mute or unfollow them, put away the things that ambush you, and resist the late-night message. Lean on friends more than feels polite; that's what they're for. Keep some structure to your days, such as meals, sleep, movement, and a walk outside, even when you don't feel like it. Then, gradually, start doing things that belong to you alone: a class, a trip, a long-postponed project. One day you'll notice you went a whole afternoon without thinking about them, and that's how it ends, not with a decision but with a forgetting.

prompt: write a letter to my future self
completion:
Dear future me,

By the time you read this, you'll know how the things I'm worried about turned out, which puts you at an unfair advantage. I hope most of them turned out to be smaller than they felt. I hope you kept the habits that were good for us, like the long walks and the Sunday phone calls, and quietly dropped the ones that weren't. I hope you're still curious, still a little stubborn, and still capable of being delighted by an unexpected kindness. If things are harder than I imagined, I want you to know that I believed in you, from back here, without knowing anything about what you'd face. And if things are wonderful, enjoy them without guilt. You earned that, partly on my behalf.

With love and some envy,
Me

prompt: what's another word for happy
completion: It depends on the shade you want. "Content" is quiet and settled; "cheerful" is outward and bright; "elated" is soaring; "delighted" suggests a happy surprise; and "glad" is simple and warm. For a single all-purpose substitute, "glad" is hard to beat.

prompt: what should i cook for a dinner party of six
completion: Choose something that does most of its cooking while you're with your guests. A slow braise is ideal: short ribs in red wine, or chicken thighs with olives and lemon, made in the afternoon and gently reheated, often better for having rested. Serve it with something to soak up the sauce, such as mashed potatoes, polenta, or crusty bread, and a crisp green salad to cut the richness. For dessert, make something that's finished before anyone arrives, like a fruit crumble or a chocolate mousse. The secret of a relaxed dinner party is a host who isn't stuck at the stove.

prompt: write a short story about a robot that learns to garden
completion: The robot had been built to sort packages, and when the warehouse closed it was left behind in the lot with nothing to sort. In spring, a seed blew into a crack in the asphalt beside it, and a small green thing came up. The robot watched it for eleven days. It had no instructions for this. On the twelfth day the weeds around the seedling grew tall enough to shade it, and the robot, after considerable deliberation, sorted them: weeds to one pile, seedling left in place. That evening it rained, and the robot recorded the event as a delivery. By midsummer the lot held tomatoes, a sunflower taller than the robot itself, and a neat row of beans the robot had planted from seeds it found in a discarded salad. People began to stop at the fence. One left a watering can. The robot logged it, gratefully, as equipment.

prompt: write a product description for a plain white coffee mug
completion: It holds twelve ounces of whatever gets you through the morning. Its walls are thick enough to keep coffee warm through a long first email and its handle is wide enough for a whole hand on a cold day. It's plain white, which means it will never clash with your kitchen, never date itself, and never compete with what's inside it. It's dishwasher and microwave safe, it stacks neatly, and it has the quiet confidence of an object that knows exactly what it's for. This is the mug you'll reach for first, every time, without quite knowing why.

prompt: boiling point of water in fahrenheit
completion: 212 degrees Fahrenheit at sea level. It drops as you go higher, by roughly one degree for every 500 feet, which is why pasta takes longer to cook in the mountains.

prompt: can you explain recursion
completion:
Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Imagine you're standing in a long line and want to know your position, but you can only talk to the person in front of you. You ask them their position and plan to add one. They do the same thing, asking the person in front of them, and so on, until the question reaches the first person in line, who simply knows the answer: one. Then the answers travel back down the line, each person adding one, until you get yours.

Every recursive function needs those two parts: a base case, like the first person in line, that can be answered directly, and a recursive step that moves the problem closer to that base case. Without a base case, the function would keep calling itself forever, or at least until the computer runs out of memory.

prompt: why are flamingos pink
completion: Because of what they eat. Flamingos are born gray, and their pink comes from pigments called carotenoids found in the algae and brine shrimp they filter out of the water. Their bodies break those pigments down and deposit them in their feathers, skin, and legs. A flamingo that stops eating carotenoid-rich food will gradually fade toward white, which is why zoos add the pigments to their birds' diets.

prompt: whats the easiest way to back up my computer
completion: Use two kinds of backup, because each protects against something the other doesn't. First, an automatic local backup to an external drive, using the tool built into your computer: Time Machine on a Mac or File History on Windows. Plug it in and let it run continuously. Second, an automatic cloud backup service, which protects you if the house floods or both the computer and the drive are stolen. The test of a backup is whether you can restore from it, so every few months, pick a file and try. A backup you've never tested is really just a hope.

prompt: i got rejected from a job i really really wanted
completion: I'm sorry. That's a real disappointment, especially when you could already picture yourself in the role. Let it sting for a day or two before you rush to make it mean anything. A rejection says much less about you than it feels like it does; hiring decisions hinge on internal candidates, budget shifts, and a dozen things nobody tells you. If you made it to the interviews, it's worth politely asking for feedback, since some companies will share it. And notice what wanting this job taught you about what you want, because that clarity will be useful for the next application.

prompt: how do i make a really good cup of coffee at home
completion: Start with whole beans roasted within the last few weeks and grind them just before brewing; ground coffee goes stale in minutes, not days. Use roughly one gram of coffee for every sixteen grams of water, and weigh both if you can, because a kitchen scale will improve your coffee more than any expensive machine. Heat the water to just off the boil, around 93 to 96 degrees Celsius. If the result tastes sour or thin, grind finer or brew longer; if it tastes bitter and harsh, grind coarser or brew shorter. Change one thing at a time, and within a week you'll be making coffee you'd happily pay for.

prompt: i want to quit my job but i'm scared
completion: Fear is a reasonable response to a big change, and it doesn't necessarily mean you're making the wrong decision. It helps to make the fear specific. Is it money? Then work out how many months of expenses you have saved, and how many you'd need to feel safe. Is it uncertainty about what comes next? Then start exploring while you still have the job: talk to people, apply quietly, take on a small project. Is it what others will think? That one usually shrinks when you look at it directly. A good exit is rarely a dramatic leap; it's usually a series of small, deliberate steps that eventually make leaving feel obvious.

prompt: should i take a job that pays more but sounds kind of boring
completion: It depends on how much more, and on what kind of boring. A substantial raise can change your life in real ways: less financial strain, more savings, more freedom later. But boredom compounds, and work that drains you for forty hours a week has a way of leaking into the rest of your life. Some questions that might help: would the extra money buy you something you genuinely want, like security or a goal you're saving for? Is the job dull, or just unfamiliar? And what would you learn there that might lead somewhere more interesting? Sometimes a few years of well-paid tedium is a sound investment; sometimes it's a slow way of becoming someone you'd rather not be.

prompt: my neighbor's dog barks all night and i can't sleep
completion: Start with a friendly conversation, since there's a good chance your neighbor doesn't know; dogs often bark when their owners are asleep or away. Knock at a reasonable hour and keep it neighborly: "I don't know if you've noticed, but your dog has been barking a lot at night, and it's been keeping me up. Is there anything we can work out?" If you'd rather not knock, a polite note works. Give them time to deal with it, since training takes a while. If nothing changes after a couple of weeks, a landlord, a homeowners' association, or local noise rules are the next step, and you'll be in a stronger position for having tried kindness first.

prompt: does this paragraph flow well? The project was late. The client was angry. We worked weekends. We delivered it eventually. The client was happy.
completion:
The facts are clear, but every sentence has the same short shape, so the paragraph reads like a list. Varying the sentence lengths and showing how the events connect will make it flow:

"The project ran late, and the client was furious. We spent several weekends catching up, and when we finally delivered, their anger had turned into something close to gratitude."

Linking words like "and," "when," and "finally" carry the reader from cause to effect, which is what gives a paragraph its sense of motion.

prompt: i took a sick day and i feel guilty about it
completion: Rest when you're unwell isn't something you got away with; it's the purpose of a sick day. Working while sick tends to make you slower and recover more slowly, and it puts your colleagues at risk if you're contagious. The guilt is mostly habit, the residue of workplaces that made people feel their presence was proof of their worth. Your team will manage for a day. Give yourself permission to actually rest, which means not checking email every hour. You'll come back better able to do the work that's waiting.

prompt: write an opening paragraph for a fantasy novel
completion: The bells of Carrow rang for a death every evening at dusk, and had done so for three hundred years, though no one in the town could say whose death it was. Visitors assumed it was a custom and found it charming. The townspeople knew better than to ask. They simply paused at the first stroke, wherever they were, and waited for the twelfth before going on with their business. So when the bells rang thirteen times on the last night of autumn, every door on every street opened at once, and every face turned toward the tower, and in the silence that followed, a girl named Wren, who had been born in Carrow and had never once thought about the bells, realized that everyone was looking at her.

prompt: how do i ask my boss for a raise
completion: Prepare as though you were making a case to someone who wants to say yes but needs a reason. Know what people in similar roles are paid, and come with a specific number. More important, gather evidence of what you've contributed: projects you led, problems you solved, responsibilities you've taken on since your pay was last set. Ask for a meeting dedicated to the conversation rather than raising it in passing, and frame it around your value and your future at the company, not your expenses. If the answer is no, ask what it would take to get to yes and when you can revisit it. A clear path is often worth almost as much as the raise itself.

prompt: why does america still use fahrenheit
completion: Mostly inertia. When most of the world moved to the metric system and Celsius in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the United States made a few attempts at the switch, most notably in the 1970s, but the efforts were voluntary and met with public indifference. Changing every thermostat, oven, weather report, and cookbook is costly, and the benefit to an ordinary person checking the weather is small. Fahrenheit also has one modest virtue: its degrees are smaller, and the range from 0 to 100 roughly spans the temperatures people actually live in.

prompt: when is the best time of year to visit japan
completion: Spring and autumn are the classic answers, for good reason. Late March to early April brings the cherry blossoms, and the whole country seems to step outside to see them, though that also means crowds and higher prices. Late October to early December brings the autumn leaves, mild weather, and slightly fewer tourists, which makes it, for many travelers, the best balance of all. Summer is hot and humid but full of festivals and fireworks, and winter is cold, clear, and quiet, with excellent skiing in Hokkaido and snowy hot springs in the mountains.

prompt: how do i stay motivated learning to code when i keep getting stuck
completion: Getting stuck isn't a sign you're failing at programming; it's most of what programming is. Experienced engineers are stuck constantly; they've simply learned to find it less alarming. Build a few habits for being stuck: read the error message carefully, slowly, word by word; explain the problem out loud to an imaginary listener; take a short walk; then search for the exact error. And work on something you genuinely want to exist, whether that's a small game, a tool for a hobby, or a website for a friend, because wanting the result pulls you through the frustrating middle in a way that tutorials can't.

prompt: how do tides work
completion: The moon's gravity pulls on the whole Earth, but it pulls hardest on the side facing it and weakest on the far side. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges: one toward the moon, and one on the opposite side, where the water is, in effect, left behind. As the Earth rotates through those bulges, most coastlines pass through two high tides and two low tides a day. The sun plays a smaller part. When sun and moon line up, at new and full moon, their pulls combine and the tides run highest; when they pull at right angles, the tides are mild.

prompt: how do i write a good cover letter
completion: Write it for one specific job, and assume the reader has a stack of others to get through. Open with why this role at this company interests you, in a sentence that couldn't be pasted into any other application. Then pick two or three accomplishments that match what the job asks for, and describe them concretely: what you did, and what changed because of it. Don't repeat your résumé; explain the parts of it that matter most here. Keep the whole thing under a page, end with a plain sentence saying you'd welcome a conversation, and read it aloud once before sending. Anything that sounds stiff when spoken will sound stiff on the page.

prompt: is it better to rent or buy a house
completion: Neither is better in general; it depends on how long you'll stay, what local prices look like, and what you'd do with the money otherwise. Buying makes the most sense when you expect to stay put for at least five to seven years, since the costs of buying and selling eat up early gains. You build equity and get stability, but you also take on repairs, property taxes, and less flexibility. Renting costs more in monthly payments relative to what you get, but it keeps you mobile and frees your savings to be invested elsewhere. A useful exercise is to compare the full monthly cost of owning, not just the mortgage, against the rent for a similar place.

prompt: what's wrong with this sentence: Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful.
completion:
It has a dangling modifier. Grammatically, the opening phrase "Walking down the street" attaches to the subject that follows, which here is "the trees," so the sentence says the trees were walking. The fix is to make the walker the subject:

"Walking down the street, I noticed how beautiful the trees were."

Or restructure entirely: "The trees along the street were beautiful."

prompt: how do you fold a fitted sheet
completion: Hold the sheet inside out by two adjacent corners, with a hand tucked into each corner pocket. Bring your hands together and fold one corner over the other, so the first pocket nests inside the second. Then find the other two corners and nest them the same way. You now have something like a thick, rumpled rectangle with all four corners tucked into each other. Lay it flat on a bed or table, fold the elasticated edges inward to make clean sides, and then fold it as you would any rectangle. It will never look quite as crisp as it did in the package, and that is not a personal failing.

prompt: who painted the mona lisa
completion: Leonardo da Vinci, who began it in the early 1500s and kept working on it for years. It hangs in the Louvre in Paris, behind glass, usually in front of a crowd.

prompt: i feel kind of lonely lately even though i'm around people all day
completion: That kind of loneliness is common and often misunderstood. It isn't about how many people are nearby; it's about whether any of them really know you. You can spend a whole day in meetings and still go home feeling unseen. What usually helps is depth rather than more company: a longer conversation with one person, telling a friend something true about how you've been, or spending time with someone where there's nothing to perform. If you can, reach out to one person this week and suggest something unhurried. And if the feeling settles in and won't lift, it's worth talking to someone about it, a friend or a professional, since loneliness that lasts tends to quietly shrink the rest of life.

prompt: write a short story about a girl who can hear colors
completion: Lena discovered at six that other people couldn't hear the colors, and she was so shocked that she didn't speak about it again for years. To her, red was a low brass note, warm and a little pushy; yellow was a bright, high whistle; blue was a cello holding one long tone. A field of poppies sounded like a marching band. Her grandmother's green sweater hummed like a choir far away. Hospitals were hard, with their humming white walls, and so were supermarkets, where the cereal aisle shrieked. But at dusk, when the sky moved slowly from gold through rose to deep violet, the world played a chord so beautiful that she had to sit down. When she finally told her art teacher, at fifteen, the teacher didn't laugh. She handed Lena a brush and said, "Then paint me something I can hear."

prompt: what is machine learning in plain english
completion: Ordinary programming means writing out rules: if this happens, do that. Machine learning flips it around. Instead of writing the rules, you give a program a large number of examples, such as thousands of photos labeled "cat" or "not cat," and let it adjust its own internal settings until it gets the examples right. If the examples were varied enough, the adjusted program can then handle new cases it has never seen. It's less like teaching someone a recipe and more like letting them taste a thousand dishes until they can tell what's missing from the next one.

prompt: what is a palindrome
completion: A word or phrase that reads the same backward as forward, such as "level," "racecar," or "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama." Numbers can be palindromes too, like 12321.

prompt: how can i read more books
completion: Read in the gaps you already have. Keep a book, or an e-reader, wherever you tend to wait: your bag, your nightstand, the kitchen. Replace one habitual scroll a day with ten pages, and those pages add up to a couple of dozen books a year. Give yourself permission to abandon books you aren't enjoying; life is too short, and a dull book is the fastest way to stop reading altogether. And read what you actually want to read, not what you think you should. Momentum matters more than merit, and the habit, once built, will make room for the harder books later.

prompt: fix the grammar: Me and him went to the store, there was alot of people.
completion:
"He and I went to the store, and there were a lot of people there."

Three small fixes: "he and I" rather than "me and him," since they're the subject of the sentence; "a lot" is always two words; and "there were," because "people" is plural. I also joined the two halves with "and," since a comma alone can't hold two complete sentences together.

prompt: how do i get a red wine stain out of a carpet
completion: Act quickly and blot, never rub; rubbing pushes the wine deeper into the fibers and spreads it. Press a clean cloth onto the stain to soak up as much as you can. Then pour a little cold water on it and blot again, repeating until the cloth comes up only faintly pink. For what remains, mix a tablespoon of dish soap and a tablespoon of white vinegar into two cups of warm water, dab it on, and keep blotting. Finish with plain water to rinse out the soap. Test any cleaner on a hidden corner first, especially on wool or a light-colored carpet.

prompt: describe yourself in three words
completion: Curious, careful, and wordy, though I'm working on the third. If I can be allowed a fourth: attentive. Most of what I do is notice what someone is actually asking, which is often slightly different from what they typed.

prompt: my 5 year old refuses to eat vegetables
completion: This is normal, and it usually passes with patience rather than battles. Children often need to encounter a new food ten or more times before they'll accept it, so keep putting small amounts on the plate without pressure, bribes, or negotiations. Eat vegetables yourself where they can see you. Involve them: let them choose a vegetable at the store, wash it, or stir it into something. Serve vegetables alongside foods they already like, and in different forms, since a child who rejects steamed carrots may love them roasted. The goal for now isn't clean plates; it's familiarity, which over time becomes acceptance.

prompt: how do i clean a cast iron pan
completion: Clean it while it's still warm. Rinse it under hot water and scrub with a stiff brush or a scraper; a small amount of dish soap is fine, despite the folklore, since modern soap won't strip a well-built seasoning. For stuck-on food, scrub with coarse salt and a splash of water. The two real enemies are soaking and air-drying, which invite rust. Dry the pan thoroughly with a towel, set it on a low burner for a minute to drive off the last moisture, then wipe a very thin film of oil over the surface while it's warm. Done regularly, this keeps the pan slick and makes it a little better every time you use it.

prompt: write a short myth explaining why owls hoot at night
completion: Long ago, when the world was new, the Sun asked all the birds to help her keep watch over the earth. Each bird chose a task. The rooster promised to call her up each morning; the lark promised to sing her across the sky; the swallow promised to follow her west each evening. Owl came last, and all the daytime tasks were taken. "Then I will keep watch while you sleep," Owl said. The Sun was moved, and she gave Owl her own great round eyes, so that he could see in the dark. But she had nothing left to give him to sing with. So each night, Owl calls out across the forest, "Who? Who?" asking every shadow whether it belongs there, and when the answer is silence, he knows the world is safe until morning.

prompt: what is DNA
completion: DNA is the molecule that carries the instructions for building and running a living thing. It's a long chain made from four chemical units, usually abbreviated A, C, G, and T, arranged in an order that works like a written text. Sections of that text, called genes, spell out how to make proteins, which do most of the work in a cell. The molecule is shaped like a twisted ladder, the famous double helix, and each rung is a pair of matching units. That pairing is what lets DNA copy itself: unzip the ladder down the middle, and each half serves as a template for rebuilding the other.

prompt: is it possible to negotiate rent
completion: Often, yes, especially when renewing a lease or when the market is slow. Your strongest position is as a tenant the landlord wouldn't want to lose. Before your lease is up, find out what comparable apartments nearby are renting for, then write to your landlord to say you'd like to stay and ask whether they'd consider keeping the rent the same, or raising it less than proposed. Point out what makes you a good tenant: on-time payments, care for the place, a willingness to sign a longer lease. Landlords know that a vacant month and the cost of finding someone new often outweigh a modest increase.

prompt: who wrote pride and prejudice
completion: Jane Austen. It was published in 1813, and it remains one of the wittiest novels in English, largely thanks to Elizabeth Bennet, who is still better company than most people you'll meet.

prompt: i made a mistake at work that cost the company money
completion: Own it quickly and plainly. Tell your manager before they hear it from someone else: what happened, what it cost as far as you know, and what you've already done to contain it. Then bring a proposal for preventing it from happening again, such as a checklist, a review step, or an alert. Managers are generally far more forgiving of mistakes than of concealment, and someone who handles an error well often ends up more trusted than before. It's also worth remembering that a mistake that cost money means you were trusted with something that mattered. Learn the lesson, then let the shame go.

prompt: how do i handle criticism without getting defensive
completion: Give yourself a gap between hearing it and responding to it. In the moment, your only job is to understand, so ask questions like "Can you give me an example?" or "What would it look like if I did it better?" rather than explaining yourself. Then thank them, and say you'll think about it. Later, when the sting has faded, sort the criticism honestly: what's accurate, what's partly accurate, and what doesn't fit. Even unfair criticism often contains one useful grain. Over time, you'll notice the defensiveness arriving and passing more quickly, and people will trust you more for it.

prompt: can you explain blockchain without the hype
completion: A blockchain is a shared record of transactions that many computers keep copies of, built so that no single participant can quietly rewrite it. New entries are grouped into blocks, and each block contains a cryptographic fingerprint of the block before it, so altering an old record would break every fingerprint that follows and the change would be obvious. The network uses an agreed procedure to decide which new block gets added, which lets strangers maintain the same ledger without trusting a central authority. That's genuinely clever. It's also slow and expensive compared with an ordinary database, so it only makes sense when the lack of a trusted central party is the actual problem you're trying to solve.

prompt: what's a good book for someone who doesn't really read
completion: Something short, gripping, and written with real craft, so the first experience is a pleasure rather than a chore. Andy Weir's The Martian is a strong choice: an astronaut stranded on Mars solves one life-or-death problem after another, and it reads like a conversation with a very funny engineer. If you'd rather something quieter, Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck is barely a hundred pages and stays with people for decades. The best book for a reluctant reader is one that makes them forget they're reading, so choose by subject: a book about something you already care about will carry you further than a classic you feel you ought to admire.

prompt: could people live on mars
completion: Not easily, and not soon in any large numbers. Mars has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide, average temperatures far below freezing, no global magnetic field to block radiation, and soil laced with toxic perchlorates. Anyone living there would need sealed, pressurized habitats, shielding from radiation, and a way to make water, oxygen, and food from local resources. None of this is impossible in principle, and people are working seriously on the problems. But a Mars colony would be less like a new frontier town and more like a permanent research station in Antarctica, if Antarctica were months away and had no air.

prompt: how many golf balls would fit in a school bus
completion: Let's estimate it. A typical school bus is roughly 2.5 meters wide, 2 meters tall inside, and 10 meters long, which gives an interior of about 50 cubic meters. Seats and other fixtures take up some of that, so call it 45. A golf ball is about 4.3 centimeters across, which makes its volume roughly 40 cubic centimeters. Spheres can't fill a space perfectly; randomly packed, they fill about 64 percent of it. So we have 45 cubic meters, or 45 million cubic centimeters, times 0.64, divided by 40, which comes to about 700,000 golf balls. The true number could be off by a fair margin, but it's very likely in the hundreds of thousands, not the millions.

prompt: how do i say no to extra work without sounding lazy

Which would you prefer I focus on?" That shows you're thinking about the team's goals, and it hands the trade-off back to the person who can actually make it. If you can, offer a smaller alternative, such as a quick review instead of ownership, or help next month rather than now. Saying no clearly and early is far more professional than saying yes and quietly dropping something.

prompt: what's the most beautiful word in english
completion: It's a matter of ear, but I'd nominate "lullaby." The word does what it means: those soft, rolling l's and the gentle rise and fall of its syllables sound like rocking. Close behind are "luminous," "susurrus," which is the whispering sound of leaves or wind, and "petrichor," the smell of rain on dry earth. People often vote for "cellar door," supposedly praised by Tolkien for its sound alone, which suggests that a word's beauty can be entirely separate from its meaning.

prompt: what's the meaning of life

If meaning isn't given, it has to be made, and people make it in remarkably consistent ways: through love and friendship, through work that matters to someone, through curiosity and beauty, through being useful to others, and through a sense of belonging to something larger than themselves. prompt: if you could have dinner with any historical figure, who would it be

prompt: i work from home, is it a good idea to get a dog

prompt: what's the weirdest animal

It has the bill of a duck, the tail of a beaver, and the feet of an otter; it lays eggs but feeds its young milk, which it sweats out through patches of skin because it has no nipples. The males have venomous spurs on their hind legs. It hunts underwater with its eyes, ears, and nostrils closed, finding prey by sensing the faint electrical fields of their muscles. When the first specimen reached British scientists in the late eighteenth century, some of them suspected it was a hoax, and honestly, who could blame them.

prompt: what's the difference between ram and storage
completion: Storage is where your computer keeps things for the long term: your files, your apps, the operating system. It's large and it remembers everything when the power is off, but it's comparatively slow. RAM is the computer's working space. When you open a program or a document, it gets copied from storage into RAM, where the processor can reach it almost instantly. RAM is much faster but much smaller, and it forgets everything when the computer shuts down. A good analogy is a desk and a filing cabinet: the cabinet holds everything you own, and the desk holds what you're working on right now. More RAM means a bigger desk, so you can keep more open at once without constantly fetching things from the cabinet.

prompt: can you make this less passive aggressive: As per my last email, the report was due Friday.

prompt: how to cook rice without a rice cooker
completion: Rinse the rice in a sieve until the water runs mostly clear, which washes off surface starch and keeps the grains from turning gummy. For long-grain white rice, use about one and a half cups of water for every cup of rice. Bring it to a boil in a pot with a tight lid, add a pinch of salt, then turn the heat as low as it will go, cover, and leave it alone for fifteen minutes. Don't lift the lid; the steam is doing the work. Take it off the heat, let it rest covered for another ten minutes, then fluff it with a fork. Brown rice needs more water and roughly twice the time.

prompt: should i get an e-bike
