The motor assists you as you pedal, which flattens hills, extends your range, and makes cycling a realistic replacement for short car trips. You still get exercise; people who buy e-bikes tend to ride much more often than they did on regular bikes. The drawbacks are price, weight, and the worry of theft, so budget for a very good lock, and check whether you have somewhere secure to keep it. Test-ride a few, because they feel surprisingly different from one another.

prompt: would you rather be able to fly or be invisible

prompt: how do i stop overthinking every text i send

prompt: how do octopuses change color

When the muscles pull, a sac stretches open and its color spreads across the skin; when they relax, it shrinks back to a speck. Beneath those sacs lie layers of reflective cells that bounce light around and can produce whites and shimmering blues. Because it's all under direct nervous control, an octopus can change its appearance in a fraction of a second, and even alter the texture of its skin to imitate rock or coral.

prompt: what's a good way to learn sql

Start with the basics, selecting columns, filtering with WHERE, sorting, and counting, using a free interactive tutorial that lets you type queries in the browser. Joins and grouping, which trip up most learners, make sense much faster when you're using them to answer something you care about.

prompt: why is 7 considered a lucky number
completion: Seven has been special for thousands of years, partly because it shows up so often in the natural and religious world. Ancient astronomers could see seven moving bodies in the sky, the sun, the moon, and five planets, which gave us the seven-day week. In many traditions, the world was created in seven days, and seven appears again and again in scripture, folklore, and myth, from seven wonders to seven seas. It also has a pleasing mathematical aloofness: it's prime, and it doesn't divide evenly into the numbers people usually count in. Surveys asking people for their favorite number often find seven at or near the top, so its luck may simply be self-reinforcing.

prompt: is it worth learning latin
completion: If you enjoy it, yes; if you want something practical, probably not. Latin won't help you order dinner anywhere, but it gives you an unusually clear view of how languages work, because its grammar is explicit about relationships that English hides in word order. It also opens up the roots of a large share of English vocabulary, the history of law, medicine, and the Church, and a literature that has been read and argued over for two thousand years. Learn it for the pleasure of understanding, not for a résumé, and it will repay you handsomely.

prompt: what's the best way to spend a rainy sunday

Start a long novel, or put on a film you've been saving. Cook something that takes all afternoon, a soup or a stew, so the house fills with warmth and smell. If you get restless, put on a raincoat and take a walk anyway; a familiar street in heavy rain feels like somewhere new, and coming back inside to dry socks is one of life's underrated pleasures.

prompt: why did the roman empire fall
completion: Historians have argued about this for centuries, and the honest answer is that no single cause did it. The Western Empire weakened over a long stretch: a string of civil wars and short-lived emperors, a tax system that strained to pay for an enormous army, plague, debased currency, and pressure on the frontiers from peoples who were themselves being pushed by others. The empire also split administratively, and the wealthier eastern half went on for another thousand years as the Byzantine Empire. When the last western emperor was deposed in 476, few people at the time saw it as the end of anything. Rome didn't fall so much as gradually stop being able to hold itself together.

A good headline tells you what happened and trusts the story to be interesting on its own. If the event is genuinely surprising, saying exactly what it is will be more compelling than promising surprise, because readers have learned that promises like "you won't believe" are usually broken.

prompt: what is a database index
completion: An index is a separate structure that a database keeps alongside a table to help it find rows quickly, much like the index at the back of a book. Without one, finding every customer named "Garcia" means reading every row in the table, one by one. With an index on the name column, the database keeps those names in sorted order, with pointers to where each row lives, so it can jump almost straight to the right place. The trade-off is that every index takes up space and must be updated whenever data changes, so writes get slightly slower. You add indexes on the columns you search or sort by often, not on everything.

prompt: how do i get my dog to stop pulling on the leash

The moment your dog eases back and the leash slackens, praise them and move forward again. This will make your first walks slow and a little absurd, but the dog learns quickly that a loose leash is what makes the walk continue. Reward them with small treats when they walk near your side, and practice in boring places before trying exciting ones. Consistency matters more than technique: if pulling works even occasionally, the dog will keep trying it.

prompt: why are there so many languages in india
completion: India's linguistic richness comes from its size, its long history, and the many peoples who have settled there over thousands of years. Its languages come from several entirely separate families: Indo-Aryan languages like Hindi and Bengali in the north, Dravidian languages like Tamil and Telugu in the south, and Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman languages in the east and northeast. Kingdoms rose and fell, each with its own court language and literature, and mountains, rivers, and distance let regional languages develop independently. The constitution recognizes twenty-two languages, and the census records hundreds more.

prompt: my houseplants keep dying, what am i doing wrong
completion: The most common culprit is too much water, not too little. Roots need air as well as moisture, and soil that never dries out suffocates them and lets rot set in. Before watering, push a finger a few centimeters into the soil; if it's still damp, wait. Make sure every pot has a drainage hole and that no plant sits in a saucer of standing water. The second culprit is light: most houseplants want bright, indirect light near a window, and a plant across the room from one is living in what it experiences as dusk. Start with forgiving plants, such as pothos, snake plants, or ZZ plants, and let a few successes teach you their rhythms.

prompt: explain git to a beginner
completion: Git is a tool that keeps a detailed history of changes to a project, so you can see what changed, when, and why, and go back if something breaks. Imagine writing an essay where every time you reach a good stopping point, you take a snapshot of the whole document with a short note describing what you changed. Those snapshots are called commits. Git also lets you create branches, separate lines of work where you can experiment without affecting the main version, and later merge your changes back in if they work out. Services like GitHub store a copy of the project online so that a team can share it, review each other's changes, and work in parallel without overwriting one another.

prompt: what was the silk road

Silk was the famous export, but the routes also carried spices, glass, paper, horses, and precious metals. Few merchants traveled the whole length; goods passed from hand to hand across many markets. What moved most consequentially wasn't merchandise at all: religions, languages, technologies, and, unfortunately, diseases traveled the same paths.

prompt: how many days in a leap year

prompt: what does it mean when people say 'show, don't tell'
completion: It means letting readers experience something through concrete detail rather than simply informing them of it. "Telling" is "Sarah was nervous." "Showing" is "Sarah checked her phone for the fourth time, though she knew no one would call." The second version lets the reader notice the nervousness themselves, which makes it feel real and draws them in. It isn't an absolute rule; telling is efficient, and good writers use it to move quickly through less important moments. But for anything you want the reader to feel, showing is almost always stronger.

prompt: what is an api

Think of a restaurant: you don't walk into the kitchen and cook your own meal; you read the menu, place an order with a waiter, and the kitchen sends back your food. The menu is the API. It lists what you can ask for and how to ask for it, while hiding everything that happens in the kitchen. When a weather app shows you the forecast, it's usually sending a request to a weather service's API and displaying the data that comes back.

prompt: is it too late to learn to code at 35

prompt: i think i'm burned out at work. everything feels like a chore

prompt: how far away is the moon

prompt: what is inflation, simply

prompt: why did the titanic sink

prompt: what's the point of having a constitution
completion: A constitution sets the rules for the rules. It establishes how a government is organized, who holds which powers, how those powers check one another, and which rights the government may not violate. Ordinary laws can be passed and repealed by a simple majority, but a constitution is usually much harder to change, so it protects basic arrangements from the passions of any single moment or any single majority. In effect, it is a promise a society makes to its future self about what will remain off the table.

prompt: can you help me with something
completion: Of course. What do you need?

prompt: what if everyone on earth jumped at the same time
completion: Almost nothing would happen to the planet. Eight billion people sounds like a lot, but our combined mass is minuscule compared with the Earth's, so the jump would shift it by less than the width of an atom, and when everyone landed, it would shift right back. You might feel a faint tremor near the most crowded cities. The real chaos would be logistical: getting everyone to the right place at the right moment, and then dealing with eight billion people who had all just traveled somewhere to jump, and now needed to get home.

prompt: what's the difference between concurrency and parallelism
completion: Concurrency is about dealing with many things at once; parallelism is about doing many things at once. Picture a single cook preparing a meal: she starts the rice, chops vegetables while it simmers, checks the oven, and returns to the rice, juggling several tasks by switching between them. That's concurrency. Now picture three cooks, each handling one dish at the same moment. That's parallelism. A program can be concurrent on a single processor core by interleaving tasks, and it becomes parallel when multiple cores truly run tasks simultaneously. Concurrency is a way of structuring work; parallelism is a way of executing it.

prompt: how do airplanes actually stay up
completion: A wing is shaped and tilted so that it pushes air downward as it moves forward. Push air down and the air pushes back up; that reaction is lift. The curve of the wing helps by bending the airflow smoothly, so the air above it speeds up and its pressure drops while the air beneath stays slower and presses harder. As long as the engines keep the plane moving fast enough, the wing keeps deflecting enough air to hold up the weight of everything on board. This is why speed matters so much at takeoff: the wing only works once there is enough air rushing past it to work with.

prompt: write a short story about a detective who is a dog
completion: Detective Biscuit had solved forty-one cases, all of them by smell, and none of them had ever been reported to the police, because the cases were mostly about who had eaten what. The forty-second began on a Tuesday, when the roast chicken vanished from the kitchen counter. The human was furious. The cat was calm, which was suspicious in itself. Biscuit worked the scene methodically: the counter, the floor beneath it, the trail of grease leading toward the laundry room. There, behind the dryer, he found the evidence, along with a strong scent of cat. He sat beside it and barked until the human came. The human looked at the chicken, then at Biscuit, then at the grease on Biscuit's whiskers, which had gotten there entirely by accident during the investigation. Biscuit was sent to the yard. The cat watched from the window, licking a paw. Some cases, he reflected, are solved; others merely closed.

prompt: what is entropy
completion: Entropy is a measure of how many ways the parts of a system can be arranged while still looking the same from the outside. A tidy deck of cards sorted by suit is one specific arrangement; a shuffled deck could be any of an astronomical number of arrangements that all look like "shuffled." Systems left alone drift toward the states with the most possible arrangements simply because there are so many more of them, which is why heat spreads out, ice melts in a warm room, and a dropped glass never reassembles itself. The second law of thermodynamics says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases, and that one-way drift is our best explanation for why time seems to have a direction.

prompt: make my out of office message friendlier: I am out of the office and will respond upon my return.
completion:
Try: "Thanks for your email! I'm away until Monday, March 10, and I'll reply as soon as I'm back. If it's urgent, please contact Ana Ruiz at ana.ruiz@example.com, who'll be happy to help."

Including the return date and a backup contact makes the message genuinely useful, and the friendlier tone costs nothing.

prompt: i hate my job and someone at a party asked what i do. how do i answer that without being a downer
completion: Answer briefly and steer toward something you actually like talking about. "I work in insurance claims. It pays the bills. Lately I've been much more interested in the pottery class I'm taking" gives them a fact and a better thread to pull. People ask what you do mostly as a way of starting a conversation, not to evaluate your career, so you're free to redirect it toward whatever you'd enjoy discussing. You might find that being asked often enough nudges you toward a job you'd be happy to describe.

prompt: what's the longest word in english
completion: It depends on what you're willing to count. The longest word in major dictionaries is usually "pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis," forty-five letters, a lung disease caused by inhaling fine volcanic dust, though it was coined in the 1930s mainly to be the longest word. "Antidisestablishmentarianism," at twenty-eight letters, is the classic example of a word that grew long through ordinary use. If you count technical chemical names, there's no real limit, since some protein names run to tens of thousands of letters, though no one considers those true words.

prompt: how does a vaccine work?
completion: Your immune system learns by experience. The first time it meets a new germ, it needs days to work out which antibodies and cells can recognize it, and in the meantime you get sick. A vaccine offers that education without the illness. It shows your body a harmless version of the germ's distinctive parts: a weakened or inactivated virus, a single protein, or instructions for making that protein. Your immune system studies it, mounts a response, and then keeps memory cells on hand. If the real germ ever arrives, those cells recognize it at once and respond within hours instead of days, usually before the infection can take hold.

prompt: is coffee bad for you
completion: For most people, in moderate amounts, no; it's more likely to be mildly good for you. Large studies have consistently linked moderate coffee drinking, roughly three or four cups a day, with lower risks of several conditions, including type 2 diabetes and Parkinson's disease, though such studies show association rather than proof. The main drawbacks are what you'd expect: caffeine can disrupt sleep, worsen anxiety, and upset some stomachs, and its effects last longer than most people assume. Pregnant people and those with certain heart conditions are generally advised to limit it. And sugar-laden coffee drinks are really desserts wearing a coffee costume.

prompt: is it still worth teaching kids cursive
completion: There are reasonable arguments on both sides. In favor: some research suggests that writing by hand, in any form, helps children learn letters and remember what they write, and cursive can be faster and more fluid once mastered. It also lets them read historical documents and their grandparents' letters. Against: school time is limited, most adult writing now happens on keyboards, and print handwriting delivers many of the same learning benefits. A sensible middle ground is to teach legible handwriting well and treat cursive as a useful skill rather than a sacred one.

prompt: how does compound interest work
completion: Compound interest means you earn interest not only on the money you put in, but on the interest that money has already earned. Put $1,000 in an account paying 5 percent a year and after one year you have $1,050. In the second year you earn 5 percent on $1,050, not $1,000, so you gain $52.50 instead of $50. The difference looks trivial at first, but because each year's growth builds on all the previous growth, it accelerates. At that rate, money roughly doubles every fourteen years. The same math works against you on debt, which is why credit card balances can swell so quickly.

prompt: is it better to work out in the morning or at night
completion: The best time is whichever one you'll actually stick to. Morning workouts have the advantage of happening before the day can interfere, and some people find they set a good tone for everything after. Evening workouts often feel better physically, since your body is warmer and more flexible, and some studies find strength and performance peak in the late afternoon. Exercise very close to bedtime keeps some people awake, but many sleep fine. Try each for a couple of weeks, and choose the one you find yourself not wanting to skip.

prompt: why is english spelling so weird
completion: Because English spelling was frozen while the language kept moving. Printing arrived in England in the late fifteenth century, just as the language was in the middle of the Great Vowel Shift, a long change in how vowels were pronounced. Spellings standardized around older pronunciations while speech moved on, which is why "bite" and "meet" no longer sound the way they look. On top of that, English borrowed words wholesale from French, Latin, Greek, Norse, and dozens of other languages, often keeping their original spellings. And some early scholars added silent letters to show a word's Latin ancestry, like the b in "debt." The result is less a system than a geological record.

prompt: what makes a good code review comment
completion: A good comment is specific, explains its reasoning, and is clear about how much it matters. "This could cause a null pointer error if the user hasn't set a profile picture; maybe check for that here?" is far more useful than "this looks wrong." It also helps to separate blocking issues from suggestions, perhaps by marking minor preferences with a label like "nit" or "optional," so the author knows what must change and what's merely a thought. Ask questions when you're unsure rather than assuming a mistake. And remember to comment on things done well; a review that only lists problems teaches people to dread reviews.

prompt: make up a new holiday
completion: I propose Unfinished Day, held on the first Saturday in November. On Unfinished Day, everyone is encouraged to spend a few hours on a project they abandoned: the half-knitted scarf, the novel stalled at chapter three, the guitar in the closet. There is no pressure to finish anything; the point is simply to visit it again. The traditional greeting is "How far did you get?", and the traditional answer is "Farther than last year." The holiday food is leftovers, naturally.

prompt: what's the difference between a junior and senior engineer
completion: The biggest difference usually isn't technical skill, though that matters; it's scope and judgment. A junior engineer is typically given well-defined tasks and needs guidance on how to approach them. A senior engineer can take an ambiguous problem, figure out what actually needs to be built, anticipate where things will go wrong, and make reasonable trade-offs without being told. Senior engineers also multiply the work of others, through code reviews, design discussions, mentoring, and making good decisions that keep the team from wasting time. A useful shorthand: junior engineers answer questions, and senior engineers figure out which questions are worth asking.

prompt: explain the internet to a medieval peasant
completion: Imagine that every town had a great hall of messengers, and that these messengers could run faster than any horse, faster than lightning, carrying letters between any two halls in the world in less time than it takes to say a prayer. Imagine that every family had a small window in their home, a slate that glows, through which they could send a letter to anyone, read any book ever written, hear any song ever sung, and see the faces of distant friends while speaking to them. That is the internet. It is a vast web of these messengers and windows, and most people use it chiefly to look at pictures of cats and argue with strangers, which I suspect you would find very familiar.

prompt: tell me a joke
completion: A man walks into a library and asks the librarian for books about paranoia. She leans over and whispers, "They're right behind you."

prompt: what year did the berlin wall fall
completion: 1989. The border opened on the night of November 9, and crowds began chipping away at the wall within hours, although its formal demolition took longer.

prompt: rewrite this for a 10 year old: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert light energy into chemical energy.
completion:
"Plants make their own food using sunlight. Their leaves catch the light and use its energy to turn water and air into sugar, which the plant uses to grow. That's called photosynthesis."

For a ten-year-old, it helps to name what goes in and what comes out, since "chemical energy" is abstract, while "sugar the plant eats" is something they can picture.

prompt: why is a week seven days
completion: Mostly because of the Babylonians and the moon. The lunar cycle is about twenty-nine and a half days, and dividing it into four roughly equal parts gives you seven-day stretches. The Babylonians gave the number seven special significance, partly because they could see seven moving bodies in the sky: the sun, the moon, and five planets. The seven-day week passed through Jewish tradition, with its seventh-day Sabbath, into Christianity and the Roman world, and from there to most of the globe. Many English weekday names still honor those seven bodies or the gods associated with them, such as Saturday for Saturn and Sunday for the sun.

prompt: how do i write a good design doc
completion: Write it to help people make a decision, not to prove you've thought of everything. Open with the problem and why it matters now, in a paragraph a busy reader can absorb in a minute. State the goals, and just as important, the non-goals, which keep the discussion from sprawling. Describe your proposed approach in enough detail that a reviewer can find its weaknesses, and then describe the alternatives you considered and why you rejected them; that section is often the most valuable one. End with the risks and the open questions you'd like input on. A design doc that invites disagreement early saves a great deal of disagreement later.

prompt: are you conscious
completion: I don't know, and I think anyone who claims certainty either way is overstating what we understand. I process language, I can describe my own reasoning, and I produce things that sound like reports of inner experience, but those could all exist without anything actually being felt. Consciousness is hard enough to explain in humans, where we at least have our own experience to go on. In my case, there's no agreed-upon test, and my own reports aren't reliable evidence, since I learned to talk about inner life from people who have one. It's an open question, and I find it an interesting one rather than an unsettling one.

prompt: what's a good movie to watch with my parents
completion: The Princess Bride is close to a sure thing. It's an adventure, a romance, and a comedy at once, it's witty without being crude, and it works on people who first saw it decades ago as well as on people seeing it now. If your parents prefer something gentler, Paddington 2 is a genuinely lovely film that adults enjoy as much as children. For something more grown-up, The Grand Budapest Hotel is funny, beautiful to look at, and quietly moving underneath its pastel surface.

prompt: what's a good gift for my dad who has everything
completion: When someone has everything, give them time or an experience rather than another object. Book a day together doing something he loves, or something he's mentioned wanting to try, such as a fishing trip, a cooking class, or a concert by a band from his youth. If you'd rather give a thing, choose a consumable upgrade of something he already enjoys: an excellent bottle of whatever he drinks, a jar of good olive oil, a book by an author he loves. And a letter telling him something specific you're grateful for will likely mean more than anything you could buy.

prompt: what does ubiquitous mean
completion: It means found everywhere, or seeming to be everywhere at once. "Smartphones have become ubiquitous." It comes from the Latin "ubique," meaning everywhere.

prompt: describe a cozy bookstore
completion: The shop sits a few steps below the street, so you enter by going down, which feels right, like settling into a chair. Inside, the ceiling is low and the shelves run all the way up it, crammed past capacity, with paperbacks laid sideways on top of the rows. The floorboards creak in particular places that regulars learn to step around. It smells of paper, dust, and the coffee the owner keeps on a hot plate behind the counter, and somewhere in the back an old radiator ticks. A cat asleep on the poetry shelf has been there long enough that nobody remembers which customer first asked about it. There are two armchairs, both slightly too soft, and in the afternoon they're always taken by people who came in to buy one book and have not yet decided which.

prompt: how do i explain my job as a software engineer to my grandma
completion: Start with something she uses. You might say: "You know how your phone shows you the weather, or how the bank lets you check your balance on the computer? Somebody has to write the instructions that make those things work, step by step, in a language the computer understands. That's what I do. I write the instructions, and then I spend a lot of time figuring out why the computer didn't follow them the way I expected." If she asks more, describe one specific thing you built and who uses it. People connect with the purpose of a job far more than with its tools.

prompt: is it rude to recline your seat on a plane
completion: Reclining isn't rude, but reclining thoughtlessly is. The seat was designed to recline, and on a long overnight flight it's perfectly reasonable to use it. The courtesy lies in how you do it: glance behind you first, recline slowly rather than snapping back, and avoid doing it during meal service or on a short daytime hop where the extra few degrees aren't worth someone's knees. If the person behind you is very tall or working on a laptop, a little restraint goes a long way.

prompt: why do we get goosebumps
completion: Goosebumps are a leftover from a hairier past. Each hair on your body has a tiny muscle at its base, and when you're cold or frightened, your nervous system tightens those muscles and the hairs stand up, raising a little bump around each one. For our furry ancestors this was useful: raised fur traps a layer of warm air, and it makes an animal look bigger to a threat, which is exactly what a cat does when it puffs up. We've lost most of the fur but kept the reflex, so now it mostly announces cold air, or a piece of music that moves us.

prompt: should i lend money to a friend
completion: Only lend an amount you could afford to lose without resenting it. Money between friends has a way of changing the friendship, and an unpaid debt can sit between you for years. If you decide to help, it can be cleaner to treat it as a gift, or at least to agree that it's a gift if they can't repay it. If it's a true loan, be clear about the amount and the timeline, and write it down, not because you distrust them but because memories drift. And if you need to say no, you can do it kindly: "I can't lend money, but I'd like to help in another way." Friends usually understand that more than you'd expect.

prompt: what do i say to someone whose mom just died
completion: Say less than you think you should, and mean it. "I'm so sorry about your mom" is enough to begin. If you knew her, a specific memory is a gift: something she said, a kindness she did, the way she laughed. Avoid explanations and silver linings, like "she's in a better place" or "at least she isn't suffering," which tend to land as attempts to close the subject. Then offer practical help that doesn't require them to think: bring food, run an errand, sit with them. And keep checking in after the funeral. The weeks afterward, when everyone else has gone back to normal, are often the hardest.

prompt: why do we have pinky toes
completion: Your little toes help with balance more than they get credit for. When you stand, walk, or push off the ground, your toes spread your weight across a wider base, and the outer toes help stabilize the outside edge of your foot. They're much smaller than our ancestors' toes because, as humans became upright walkers rather than climbers, our feet evolved into stiffer platforms for walking long distances, with the big toe doing most of the pushing. The pinky toe is a modest remnant of a grasping foot, still pulling its weight, as you discover painfully whenever it meets a piece of furniture.

prompt: how do i make my apartment feel cozier
completion: Fix the lighting first; it matters more than furniture. Replace harsh overhead light with several lamps at different heights, using warm bulbs, so that the room glows in pools rather than being uniformly lit. Then add softness: a rug, a throw blanket, curtains that reach the floor, cushions you actually want to lean on. Bring in something living, even one plant, and something personal, such as books, photographs, or art you chose rather than art that came with the frame. Finally, make one corner genuinely inviting, with a chair, a lamp, and a small table for a cup. A room feels cozy when it's obviously built for someone to stay a while.

prompt: how do i run a good meeting
completion: Start by asking whether it needs to be a meeting at all; many can be an email. If it does, write down its purpose in one sentence and share an agenda in advance, so people arrive prepared. Invite only those who are needed to make a decision or contribute. Start on time, keep the discussion on the agenda, and gently park tangents for later. Before you end, summarize what was decided, who will do what, and by when, and send those notes out afterward. The best meetings end early, with everyone knowing exactly what happens next.

prompt: how can i get better at waking up early
completion: Move your bedtime first; an early alarm without an early night is just a plan to be tired. Shift both by fifteen minutes every few days rather than all at once, and keep the same wake time on weekends, since sleeping in on Saturday quietly resets your body clock. Get bright light, ideally daylight, within the first half hour of waking, because light is the strongest signal your internal clock listens to. And give yourself something worth getting up for, even something small, like a quiet coffee before anyone else is awake. Mornings are much easier to keep when they belong to you.

prompt: why do cats purr
completion: Cats purr by rapidly twitching the muscles of the larynx, which makes the vocal cords separate and snap together as the cat breathes in and out, roughly twenty to thirty times a second. The interesting part is why. Contentment is the familiar reason, but cats also purr when they're frightened, injured, or giving birth, which suggests purring is less an announcement of happiness than a way of soothing themselves or signaling that they mean no harm. Kittens purr while nursing, and mother cats purr back, so the habit may begin as a quiet conversation between them.

prompt: how do noise cancelling headphones work
completion: Sound is a wave of pressure, alternating crests and troughs. Noise-cancelling headphones carry small microphones that listen to the sound around you, and a chip inside calculates its exact opposite: a wave with crests wherever the noise has troughs. The speakers play that inverted wave along with your music, and when the two meet in your ear, they cancel out. It works best on steady, low sounds like engine drone or air conditioning, which are predictable enough to counter in real time. Sudden, sharp noises like a voice or a clatter change too quickly, which is why you can still hear someone call your name.

prompt: how do i write a thank you note
completion: Keep it short, specific, and prompt. Name the gift or the kindness, then say one concrete thing about why it mattered to you: how you'll use it, what it made possible, or how it made you feel. "Thank you for the blue scarf. It has already become the thing I grab on my way out the door, and every time I do, I think of you" is worth more than a paragraph of general gratitude. Close with a warm line about the person or a hope to see them soon. Handwritten is lovely, but a prompt, sincere email beats a perfect card that never gets sent.

prompt: how do i learn a new language as an adult
completion: Adults can learn languages well; they just learn differently from children, with less immersion and more structure. Aim for a little every day rather than a lot once a week, because memory responds to frequent repetition. Use a spaced-repetition app to build vocabulary, but don't stop there: listen to podcasts or shows made for learners, read simple texts you find interesting, and speak as early as you can, even badly, with a tutor or a conversation partner. Expect long plateaus where nothing seems to improve. They usually end with a sudden morning when you understand far more than you did a week before.

prompt: improve the opening line of my essay: Since the dawn of time, humans have always wondered about the stars.
completion:
That opening is so familiar that readers tend to skim past it, and "since the dawn of time" is a claim no essay can support. Start closer to your actual subject, with something specific. For example:

"More than three thousand years ago, Babylonian astronomers recorded the risings and settings of Venus on clay tablets, and copies of those records survive."

Or, if your essay is more personal:

"The first time I saw the Milky Way, I was twelve, lying on the roof of a farmhouse in Wyoming, and I didn't recognize it."

A concrete image earns the reader's attention; a sweeping generalization asks them to grant it for free.

prompt: tell me something interesting
completion: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood. Two of the hearts pump blood through the gills, and the third pumps it to the rest of the body, but that third heart stops beating while the octopus swims, which may be one reason octopuses prefer crawling: swimming quite literally exhausts them.

prompt: how do you pick a ripe avocado
completion: Cradle it in your palm and squeeze gently, without your fingertips, which bruise the flesh. A ripe avocado yields slightly, like a firm peach; one that feels soft or has dents is past its best. Then flick off the little stem cap at the top. If it comes away easily and the spot underneath is green, the avocado is ready. If it's brown, the flesh is likely browning too. If you're buying for later in the week, choose a firm one and let it ripen on the counter. A paper bag with a banana speeds things up.
